issues.title: Spreadsheets are laid out as printed report tables, not data
issues.detail: Each sheet has a title row, a variable number of header rows, units in a cell above the table (£ million, £ billion, per head), section-heading rows with no numbers, and footnotes underneath. The label column and first year column move between sheets (column A in some, B in others). Sheet names are inconsistent (Table_1_11, 5_1, 9.1a, Table_2_1_(c)_).
issues.impact: A naive CSV import silently gives wrong columns or mixes section headings with data rows.
issues.handling: Generic parser finds the header by looking for three or more year labels, takes the label column as the one left of the first year, treats number-free rows as section headings, and stops at the first footnote.

issues.title: Some sheets hold several tables side by side
issues.detail: Table 9.1a has the £ million block and a "per cent of identifiable expenditure" block in the same rows, both headed by the same years.
issues.impact: Reading all year columns would double the data and mix units.
issues.handling: Only the first block of years is read; a repeated year label ends the block. Not yet verified for every sheet loaded.

issues.title: Footnote markers are part of the label text and change between tables
issues.detail: "Defence(1)" in Table 4.2, "2. Defence (4)" in Table 5.2, "Total Managed Expenditure (9)" in Table 1.11. Labels also have stray spaces and typos, for example "of which:Bank of England".
issues.impact: Joining tables by label fails or silently drops rows.
issues.handling: Trailing "(n)" markers are stripped before joining; whitespace is normalised. Row labels are otherwise kept as published.

issues.title: "-" means nil, and is indistinguishable from a rounded zero or not applicable
issues.detail: Nil cells contain a hyphen. Tables also contain real zeros and, in some places, blank cells.
issues.impact: Loading "-" as 0 is usually right but cannot show "no spending" versus "not applicable".
issues.handling: Hyphens are loaded as 0. Blanks are loaded as missing.

issues.title: Departments are grouped differently in different tables
issues.detail: Table 1.11 splits MHCLG into "MHCLG - Local Government" and "MHCLG - Housing and Communities". Table 5.1 has one "Housing, Communities and Local Government" row plus a separate "Local Government" row, which is a different thing (all local authority spending including locally raised money, not central grants to councils).
issues.impact: Matching the two by name would attach council spending to a department that does not control it.
issues.handling: dim_department has a separate pesa51_name column; both MHCLG rows point at the combined row, and the "Local Government" row is deliberately left unmapped. The UI says the functional split covers the whole group.

issues.title: Total Managed Expenditure is not the sum of departments and is not cash paid out
issues.detail: TME adds debt interest, locally financed spending, depreciation and accounting adjustments. It includes non-cash items such as provisions and write-downs. The "accounting adjustments" line was -£350bn in 2021-22 and -£151bn in 2025-26.
issues.impact: A reader adding up department bars will not reach the headline, and may read non-cash accounting as money taxpayers handed over.
issues.handling: The UI states the difference next to the headline. Department totals are labelled as TME basis.

issues.title: Accounting entries can make a department's spending negative
issues.detail: Energy Security and Net Zero shows £128.1bn in 2021-22, -£76.1bn in 2022-23 and -£6.9bn in 2023-24. PESA footnote 1 explains this as a change to the long-term discount rate for provisions (IFRS compliance), not a cash refund.
issues.impact: A chart of this series tells a false story of huge spending then huge negative spending.
issues.handling: Values are shown as published, and the Treasury's footnote is now shown beside the department's chart.

issues.title: Real-terms figures use a base year that moves every release
issues.detail: PESA 2026 states real terms are in 2025-26 prices using ONS GDP deflators (released 30 June 2026) for past years and OBR forecast deflators for plan years. Next year's release will rebase.
issues.impact: Real-terms numbers from different releases cannot be compared or mixed.
issues.handling: The deflator is derived from PESA's own nominal (Table 1.1) and real (Table 1.2) totals and stored per release. Derived factors carry rounding error of a few parts in 10^6.

issues.title: Past figures are restated every year
issues.detail: Chapter 3 lists "changes since PESA 2025" for 2024-25 onwards, and machinery-of-government changes move budgets between departments.
issues.impact: A time series built from different releases has breaks that look like policy changes.
issues.handling: Only PESA 2026 is loaded, so the series is internally consistent. Loading several releases will need the release id on every row (the source_file table already records it).

issues.title: Rounding means totals differ from sums of parts by a few £ million
issues.detail: Table 4.2 is in £ billion to one decimal place; the others are in whole £ million. Row sums differ from published totals by 1-5 £m.
issues.impact: Strict equality checks fail.
issues.handling: Reconciliation checks use explicit tolerances (£5m for sums, £100m between a £bn table and a £m table).

issues.title: The EU transactions section of Table 5.2 is laid out differently from the others
issues.detail: Its figures sit under rows labelled "derived as:", and a stray sub-row appears in 2021-22 that does not tie to Table 4.2.
issues.impact: Including it breaks the sub-function sum by about £2bn in earlier years.
issues.handling: EU transactions are left out of the purpose drill-down and out of the matching check. They are about 0.1% of spending.

issues.title: Table 5.1 has no outturn/plans label row
issues.detail: Unlike Table 1.11 it carries one year (2025-26) with no basis row. We treat it as outturn because Table 1.11 marks 2025-26 as outturn.
issues.impact: If this assumption were wrong, 5.1 values would be mislabelled.
issues.handling: Assumption recorded here; cross-check with Table 4.2 (which does label 2025-26 outturn) passes within £48m.

issues.title: Devolved governments' spending is mostly money from the UK block grant
issues.detail: Scottish Government, Welsh Government and Northern Ireland Executive appear as departments with £145bn combined in 2025-26. Much of it is funded by the UK Government.
issues.impact: Showing them beside UK departments, or adding them to UK totals in another source, risks double counting and hides who decides the spending.
issues.handling: Grouped as "Devolved governments" in the UI. Not netted against the block grant.

issues.title: Sorting by date made search results irrelevant
issues.detail: Adding order=-public_timestamp to a keyword query returned the newest pages on GOV.UK regardless of keywords.
issues.impact: Looks like the dataset does not exist.
issues.handling: Search by relevance, then pick the release from the results.

issues.title: Organisation identifiers (slugs) do not follow current names
issues.detail: DCMS is still department-for-digital-culture-media-and-sport although renamed; department-for-culture-media-and-sport exists but is marked closed. The Scottish Government is the-scottish-government. The API lists 1,267 organisations, many closed, exempt or superseded.
issues.impact: Guessing slugs from names fails or points at a closed organisation.
issues.handling: Every mapping row is checked against the live list during the pipeline and the run fails if a slug is missing. Closed organisations are kept with their status.

issues.title: File attachments and collection members live in different parts of the JSON
issues.detail: A publication lists files under details.attachments; a collection lists its publications under links.documents. Publication titles carry the month ("March 2026").
issues.impact: Easy to miss files.
issues.handling: Fetchers read both; the month is parsed from the title.

issues.title: Files are not UTF-8 and the £ column header is garbled
issues.detail: All 14 files are Windows-1252. The amount column is headed " £ " in the file (a byte that reads as a replacement character if decoded as UTF-8). Amounts are strings with a £ sign and thousands separators.
issues.impact: Default CSV readers fail or produce nonsense and the amount column is easy to lose.
issues.handling: Decode as UTF-8, fall back to Windows-1252; find the amount column as the one whose header contains £ or a replacement character; strip symbols before parsing.

issues.title: Column names drift between months
issues.detail: "Department Family" became "Departmental Family" (July 2025), "Expense Area" gained a trailing space (December 2025) and became "Expense Area rev" (April 2026).
issues.impact: Fixed-schema loaders break on the month the name changes, or worse, lose the column silently.
issues.handling: Columns are matched on prefix, and the load stops with a clear error if any expected column is missing.

issues.title: File names do not reliably say which month they hold
issues.detail: The June 2025 file is called dft-spending-24k-jun-25.csv; the publication titled April 2026 contains a file named dft-spending-over-25000-march-2026.csv, while the March 2026 publication has a different file of the same name. Dates are text in dd/mm/yyyy form.
issues.impact: Using file names would double-count March or lose April.
issues.handling: Month comes from the publication title and is verified against every row's transaction date (check: month label matches transaction dates, 0 mismatches).

issues.title: Only payments over £25,000 are published, and credits are invisible
issues.detail: The smallest amount in the 36,915 rows is £25,002.10. Refunds, credit notes and anything under the threshold are absent, and no total for what is missing is given.
issues.impact: The files cannot be added up to a net figure or to total spending. "Top supplier" rankings leave out suppliers paid many small amounts.
issues.handling: The UI calls these "payments over £25,000" and compares the total with the accounts only as a rough indication.

issues.title: Cash payments out are not the same as accounts spending
issues.detail: The files are gross cash payments. The department's accounts are accruals-based, net of income, and remove transfers within the group. In 2025-26 payments after removing intra-group transfers were about £40.0bn, against £42.9bn of Total Managed Expenditure.
issues.impact: Reading "93%" as coverage is wrong: the two measure different things, and coverage cannot be measured this way.
issues.handling: Shown with a caveat beside the ratio. A proper reconciliation to the department's annual accounts is planned.

issues.title: Placeholders instead of descriptions and transaction numbers
issues.detail: In 3,808 rows (10.3%) the Item Text is "#", and 2,879 rows (7.8%) have "#" as the Transaction No.
issues.impact: Cannot see what a payment was for, and cannot de-duplicate on transaction number.
issues.handling: Placeholders are left as published and hidden in the UI. De-duplication uses date, supplier, amount and item text together.

issues.title: Expense types are free text that differ by entity and year
issues.detail: 608 different expense types, 579 after ignoring case and spacing ("RENT" and "Rent"). Many are cut off at 20 characters ("Mail Collection/Deli", "Curr Grt Other CG Bo"). The same thing has several names across DfT, National Highways and HS2.
issues.impact: Category totals depend on a hand-built mapping, and a reader could be misled if an item lands in the wrong group.
issues.handling: First-match regex rules map them to 12 plain-English categories. About 2% of value remains "Other / unclassified". The rules are in build_spend.py. A bug was caught in testing (Eurotunnel admin pay was classed as staff pay).

issues.title: Supplier names are inconsistent and truncated
issues.detail: 172 names differ only by upper/lower case. Legal suffixes vary (LTD, LIMITED, none). Names are cut at about 35 characters ("Department for Levelling Up, Housin"). "Network Rail", "NETWORK RAIL" and "NETWORK RAIL INFRASTRUCTURE LTD" appear separately.
issues.impact: Rankings are split across spellings and may mis-state who receives the most.
issues.handling: A normalised key (case, punctuation, common suffixes) merges 2,386 raw names into 2,055. The UI says how many spellings were merged. Merging different legal entities needs Companies House matching, which is not built yet.

issues.title: Payments between bodies in the same group are counted twice
issues.detail: DfT paid £4.7bn to National Highways and other group bodies in 2025-26; those bodies then spend the money with their own contractors, and their own payments are in the same files.
issues.impact: Summing every row overstates spending by that amount.
issues.handling: A hand-kept list of group bodies flags these payments, and the UI hides them by default with a switch. The list must be maintained for each department.

issues.title: Money leaves the data at the first recipient
issues.detail: Network Rail (£10.5bn, the largest recipient) and train operators are not in the files as spenders. Payments to local authorities likewise stop at the council.
issues.impact: "Who got the money" is not "who ultimately provided the service".
issues.handling: The UI says so beside the recipient list. Later layers (contracts, grants, local spend) can extend the trail.

issues.title: HS2's funding route is not a supplier payment
issues.detail: HS2 Limited's own spend over £25,000 is about £7.2bn in 2025-26 (it publishes its own file, loaded under Transport), but DfT's file shows only about £6m paid to HS2 Ltd. The DfT annual report and accounts 2025-26 explain why: HS2 is an arm's-length body funded by grant-in-aid, which is not a supplier invoice (cash grant-in-aid, grants and loans to all arm's-length bodies was £29.5bn in 2025-26, SOPS 3, p.164). The same accounts report £7,174m for high-speed rail including HS2 (p.18) and £7bn of HS2 additions to assets under construction (p.26), consistent with HS2 Ltd's own £7.2bn.
issues.impact: HS2 Ltd's payments appear under Transport in our totals as a separate entity, and DfT's grants to it are not in the supplier files, so adding the two would double count if the grant were ever loaded.
issues.handling: HS2 Ltd payments are kept as their own entity and treated as second-hop (intra-group) spending so they are not added twice; the explanation is shown with the page references. The grant-in-aid amount per body is in the accounts' notes and is not yet loaded.

issues.title: Possible duplicate payments
issues.detail: In 2025-26, 45 payments (about £10m in total, counting each repeat once) have exactly the same date, supplier, amount, transaction number and item text as another row; 56 across all 14 months loaded.
issues.impact: May be repeated lines in the publication or genuine repeat payments.
issues.handling: Flagged, not removed.

issues.title: Two-month publication lag and uneven last month
issues.detail: The latest file (May 2026) was published on 24 September 2026. The 2026-27 year therefore has two months. Month totals vary (April 2025 £4.9bn, other months about £2.4-4.4bn) with no explanation in the files.
issues.impact: A part-year can be mistaken for a fall in spending.
issues.handling: The UI shows months covered; the fiscal year is derived as April to March.

issues.title: Some monthly files repeat every earlier month of the year
issues.detail: The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) files in the Home Office collection are year-to-date: the April 2025 file holds January to April, May holds January to May, and so on, restarting each January. Loading every file added the same payments up to eight times.
issues.impact: Summing the files gave £104m for IOPC in the period loaded; the true figure is £18m, an overstatement of nearly six times. The Home Office's own files are not affected.
issues.handling: Rows are compared across files for each publisher; a row is kept only the first time it appears (a genuine repeat inside one file is kept). 1,473 repeated rows were removed from 15 files and are counted in spend_file.n_repeats_dropped. Fiscal year is taken from the transaction date, not the file month.

issues.title: A whole year of monthly files is bundled in one publication, mixed with other bodies
issues.detail: DfT publishes one page per month. The Home Office publishes one page per year holding twelve monthly files for the Home Office and twelve for the IOPC, with the month only in the attachment title. Some file names carry reload markers such as AL1_-_Reload, and one attachment is named with plus signs instead of spaces.
issues.impact: A fetcher built for DfT finds nothing, or takes the wrong month.
issues.handling: A second fetcher reads the month and publisher from each attachment title and names files YYYY-MM__publisher__original.

issues.title: Different columns, header spellings and byte-order marks
issues.detail: No Item Text or Postal Code columns. The amount column is headed Amount (Home Office) or padded text such as '  Spend  ' and '   Spend   ' (IOPC); the supplier column is Supplier or Supplier Name. Several Home Office files start with a UTF-8 byte-order mark that shows as stray characters in the first header.
issues.impact: Loader written for DfT fails on missing columns or reads the first column wrongly.
issues.handling: Item text and postcode are optional, amount and supplier headers are matched by name patterns, and files are read with a BOM-tolerant decoder.

issues.title: Files labelled 'over £25,000' contain smaller payments and credits
issues.detail: In 2025-26, 26.7% of Home Office lines are under £25,000 and 12 lines are negative (credits or refunds). DfT's files, by contrast, contain nothing under £25,002.
issues.impact: Departments apply the threshold differently, so totals are not comparable between departments and neither is complete.
issues.handling: The UI says what share of lines is under the threshold and that credits are present.

issues.title: Published payments cover only about a fifth of the department's reported spending
issues.detail: Payments in the files total £4.2bn in 2025-26 against £22.5bn of Total Managed Expenditure in PESA (about 19%). For DfT the equivalent figure is about 93%. The accounts show why: of £27.4bn gross spending (core department and agencies) £10.1bn is main police grants, £1.9bn police pensions top-up grant, £4.6bn other current grants and £3.3bn staff pay; only £4.4bn is purchase of goods and services, of which the files show about 95%.
issues.impact: The files must not be read as 'where the Home Office's money goes'. Most of it cannot be traced from this source.
issues.handling: A reconciliation of the accounts to the files is shown on the Home Office page (from the 2025-26 accounts, pp. 246-247, hand-transcribed and checked to the published total). Where police grant money goes after the Home Office is not covered (police and crime commissioners publish their own accounts).

issues.title: 'SYSTEM CLEARING' is a ledger label, not a purchase type
issues.detail: £632m in 2025-26 is coded SYSTEM CLEARING, including payments to IBM, Galliford Try, EE and the Ministry of Justice. These look like ordinary supplier payments recorded through a clearing account.
issues.impact: Nothing about the nature of the spending can be read from the expense type for roughly a seventh of the payments.
issues.handling: Shown as 'Clearing & accounting entries (unclear)' rather than guessed. The supplier and directorate columns still identify who was paid and who paid.

issues.title: Expense types need their own category rules
issues.detail: The Home Office uses 178 expense types, mostly UPPER CASE ('IT RUN COST', 'IN COUNTRY ESCORT', 'FM ALLOCATION CONTROL'), sharing little with DfT's vocabulary. The category rules are therefore per department with a shared fallback.
issues.impact: One rule list for all departments would misclassify. 8% of Home Office value remains unclassified, against 2.3% for DfT.
issues.handling: build_spend.py has department-specific rules tried before the shared ones. The unclassified share is a live metric.

issues.title: Many payments go to other public bodies, not to the end provider
issues.detail: Among the Home Office's largest payees in 2025-26 are the Ministry of Justice, the National Crime Agency and the Government Property Agency, together about £283m.
issues.impact: Counting them as supplier income would overstate private-sector spending and hide what the money buys.
issues.handling: Shown as published. A later step could mark recipients that are public bodies once suppliers are linked to Companies House and the GOV.UK organisation list.

issues.title: A 494 MB zip holding one very wide CSV of 5.7 million companies
issues.detail: The 'Basic Company Data' snapshot (1 October 2026) has 55 columns with inconsistent names ('RegAddress.PostCode', 'SICCode.SicText_1', 'PreviousName_1.CompanyName'), dates as dd/mm/yyyy text, and up to ten previous names per company. It is published as a single file that is replaced monthly.
issues.impact: Too big to open casually, and every column name needs care.
issues.handling: Extracted once and reduced to the 14 columns needed, as a 195 MB parquet file. DuckDB normalises the column names. Only the first three previous names are used for matching.

issues.title: Matching a payee to a company by name is not identification
issues.detail: Payment files give a free-text supplier name and, for DfT only, a postcode. 66% of 2025-26 value is linked to a company, 0.4% is ambiguous (several companies share the name), 22% finds no match (joint ventures, trading names, unincorporated bodies) and 12% looks like a public body or other non-company. Test runs produced wrong links that rules now prevent: 'Cabinet Office' matched an unrelated private company called THE CABINET OFFICE LTD; 'Greater London Authority' matched a holding company; 'NEXUS' (a Tyne and Wear public transport body) matched an unrelated NEXUS LIMITED.
issues.impact: A wrong link would attach a company's status and history to money it never received.
issues.handling: A link is made only when exactly one candidate fits. Names published with a legal form (LTD, PLC, LLP) must match it exactly; names without one may match ignoring the legal form, and are marked medium confidence. Public-body-looking names are never matched by the looser rule. Every card shows how the link was made.

issues.title: The register shows today's status of one legal entity, not the whole group or the position at the time of payment
issues.detail: Status, accounts category and incorporation date are as at the 1 October 2026 snapshot. Parent and subsidiary relationships and ultimate owners are in separate data (persons with significant control) that is not loaded, so a group's subsidiaries appear as separate recipients.
issues.impact: A supplier paid in 2025 may have since been renamed, dissolved or acquired. Group totals understate how much one owner receives.
issues.handling: Cards show the snapshot date's status and say so. The 'worth knowing' notes are context only. Group ownership is a later step.

issues.title: Joint ventures and unincorporated bodies are not on the register
issues.detail: The three largest unmatched payees in DfT's files are construction joint ventures for HS2 (about £2.9bn, £2.6bn and £1.3bn in 2025-26). A joint venture is an agreement between companies, not a company, so the register has no entry, and the payment files do not name the members.
issues.impact: Several billion pounds of the most visible spending cannot be traced to companies from these sources.
issues.handling: Shown as 'not matched to a company'. Contract notices (Contracts Finder, Find a Tender) may name the members and are the next source to try.

issues.source: Contracts Finder and Find a Tender (OCDS json)
issues.title: Strict rate limit: 12 requests, then a two-minute wait
issues.detail: Both services answer HTTP 429 ('Rate limit of 12 exceeded. Please retry after 120 seconds.') with a retry-after header once about a dozen requests arrive close together. The limit appears to be shared across the two services from one address, so probing one while downloading from the other can trigger it.
issues.impact: A naive download loop fails partway through; downloading a year of award notices (about 400 pages) takes well over an hour.
issues.handling: The fetcher paces itself at one request per 9 seconds, honours the retry time in the response, and saves one file per month so an interrupted run resumes.

issues.source: Contracts Finder and Find a Tender (OCDS json)
issues.title: Search filters do not work the way the parameter names suggest
issues.detail: A keyword or buyer parameter is silently ignored (a search for 'Home Office' returned the same notices as an unfiltered one). A publishedFrom equal to publishedTo returns nothing; the end date must be later than the start. There is no filter by buyer.
issues.impact: A reader would believe the API had no data for a department, or would load another organisation's notices as the department's.
issues.handling: All award notices are fetched in two-day windows and filtered by buyer name locally, using pipeline/buyer_map.csv.

issues.source: Contracts Finder and Find a Tender (OCDS json)
issues.title: Contract award values are lifetime values or ceilings, not spending
issues.detail: An award's value is the estimated total over the whole contract term, or the maximum for a framework. It is not what has been or will be paid in a year, and is not comparable with payment files.
issues.impact: Adding contract values to payments, or reading them as annual spend, would overstate spending several times over.
issues.handling: The UI labels contract values as whole-contract values, keeps them separate from payments, and says they are not comparable.

issues.source: Contracts Finder and Find a Tender (OCDS json)
issues.title: Notices include personal contact details
issues.detail: Each notice carries a named contact's email address and phone number.
issues.impact: Storing or showing them would put individuals' details into a public tool for no benefit.
issues.handling: The fetcher discards all contact fields before saving; only organisation names, identifiers, postcodes and award details are kept.

issues.source: Contracts Finder and Find a Tender joined to payment files
issues.title: Contracts and payments are matched by supplier name or company number
issues.detail: Payment files and contract notices share no contract reference. A supplier's contracts are matched by Companies House number where the notice gives one, otherwise by a simplified form of the name; a payment is matched to the same simplified name.
issues.impact: Different companies with similar names can be joined, and a supplier trading under another name is missed. A framework ceiling is shown in full against every supplier on the framework, so contract value cannot be added up across suppliers (department totals count each award once; supplier totals count the full value of every award the supplier is on). Payments under £25,000 and payments made before the notice year are absent.
issues.handling: The panels show contract value and cash paid side by side, never summed or divided, with the warning that they measure different things; no ratio of paid to contract value is shown.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: The spend files list invoice lines, grouped under payments over £25,000
issues.detail: April 2025 to June 2026 contains 146,483 rows but only 7,201 distinct payment numbers (up to dozens of lines each). 90% of rows are individually under £25,000 and 2,783 are credits or refunds; only 51 payments total less than £25,000 once their lines are added up.
issues.impact: Counting rows as payments overstates the number of payments about twentyfold, and 'smallest payment' or 'share under the threshold' measures are meaningless at line level.
issues.handling: Rows are kept as lines. The UI says 'invoice lines in N payments' for this department and explains the threshold applies to the payment.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: Dates and amounts come in two formats, and a column appears in only some months
issues.detail: Most months give dates as dd/mm/yyyy and amounts as '£47,358,222' text. Some months (for example July 2025) give dates as Excel day numbers (45840) and amounts as plain numbers, and add a 'Cleansed Supplier' column that is missing from other months. Files are Windows-1252 encoded.
issues.impact: Fixed-format parsers fail on the changeover month or misread an Excel day number as a year or an amount.
issues.handling: The loader accepts both date forms and both amount forms, matches columns by name, and stops with an error if a required column is missing.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: Supplier names carry an unexplained '-2WM' code, and DWP's own group names exist for only three months
issues.detail: Names such as 'MITIE FM LTD - 2WM' and 'ALEXANDER MANN SOLUTIONS LTD-2WM' carry a suffix whose meaning is not published (13 suppliers affected). In three months the 'Cleansed Supplier' column gives DWP's own parent-group name (CAPITA BUSINESS SERVICES LTD becomes CAPITA GROUP PLC).
issues.impact: The same company appears under two names, and a reader cannot tell what the code means.
issues.handling: The code is ignored when matching names, the published name is kept for display, and DWP's group name is stored but not used for linking (it would hide which legal entity was paid).

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: An account labelled 'SOCIAL CARE' holds employment programme payments
issues.detail: The account 'PURCHASE OF GOODS/SERVICES - SOCIAL CARE' (£424m in 2025-26) is paid to Restart scheme providers; the cost-centre text says 'EP CEP RESTART CPA 5A CENTRAL & WEST LONDON' and similar, naming a regional contract package area.
issues.impact: Reading the account label would tell a taxpayer that £424m was spent on social care. It was spent on helping people into work.
issues.handling: Department-specific rules classify by the cost-centre text as well as the account text. Restart payments therefore show as employment programmes.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: The payment files show about 1% of what the department spends
issues.detail: Payments in the files total £2.9bn for 2025-26 against £323.5bn of spending in DWP's accounts. £296.9bn is benefits and pensions paid to people and £12.2bn is Housing Benefit paid through councils: neither is a supplier payment. £4.9bn is staff pay. The one line that is supplier spending, goods and services of £3.3bn, is about 87% visible in the files. A further £5.2bn of grants (employment, skills and apprenticeship programmes) does not appear as supplier payments, for reasons we have not confirmed.
issues.impact: Using the payment files to describe 'where DWP's money goes' would be badly misleading.
issues.handling: The page shows benefit expenditure from DWP's statistics first and puts the payment files under 'who was actually paid' with the coverage figure and a warning.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: DWP and the Treasury disagree on whether 2025-26 is outturn or forecast, and on the total
issues.detail: The Spring Forecast 2026 tables (published March 2026) label 2025-26 as forecast: £309.1bn of benefit expenditure. PESA 2026 (July 2026) shows £323.4bn Total Managed Expenditure for DWP as outturn, which also includes administration, non-cash items and other accounting entries.
issues.impact: Two reputable sources give different figures for the same year.
issues.handling: Both are shown with their own labels and a note. A check requires benefit expenditure to be within 10% of PESA's DWP total.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: Fraud and error figures are sampled estimates, measured at different dates, and unevenly old
issues.detail: FYE 2026 overpayments are estimated at £9.9bn (3.2%) with a 95% interval of £9.1bn to £10.7bn, of which £6.8bn fraud, £2.0bn claimant error, £1.1bn official error. Each benefit is last measured in a different period: Pension Credit, Universal Credit and Housing Benefit in November 2024 to October 2025, but Attendance Allowance in 2020-21, Employment and Support Allowance in 2021-22, Jobseeker's Allowance in 2017-18 and Income Support in 2013-14. Underpayments are published separately (Table 6 onwards) and not loaded yet.
issues.impact: A high percentage for one benefit and a low one for another may reflect when and how they were measured, not real differences. The numbers are not counts of proven cases.
issues.handling: The UI shows each estimate with its interval and measurement period and marks measurements before 2023 as old. It never calls the amounts 'waste' or 'fraud losses' without saying they are estimates.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: The statistics workbooks are wide, formula-driven and use unusual layouts
issues.detail: The benefit tables run from 1948/49 to 2030/31 (about 90 columns) with formulas that refer to other sheets (so values exist only as cached results), 'of which' sub-rows, and benefit names that differ between expenditure and caseload tables ('State Pension' and 'State Pension (includes contributory and non contributory)'). The fraud and error tables store pounds although headed '(£m)', use three columns per year (estimate, lower and upper 95% bound) with the year heading above the middle one, and use symbols x, z and w for suppressed, not applicable and not yet measured.
issues.impact: Reading the wrong column, or taking '£m' at face value, gives a thousandfold error or the wrong end of the interval.
issues.handling: Loaders read cached values, treat three columns as one group, keep symbols as flags, and have a hand-kept benefit-name mapping. Checks confirm benefit lines sum to the published total and that fraud, claimant error and official error add up to the published overpayment total.

issues.title: Local authority codes differ between sources
issues.detail: ONS changed the codes of Barnsley (E08000016 to E08000038) and Sheffield (E08000019 to E08000039) in 2023. The Nomis population data still uses the old codes, while the ONS region lookup has only the new ones, so a straight join silently drops two of England's 296 districts (about 1.4m people from Yorkshire and The Humber).
issues.impact: Regional population, and so every per-head figure for that region, is understated by about a quarter.
issues.handling: The loader adds the old codes as alias rows, matched on name, and reports how many aliases were needed. A check compares our per-head figures with the Treasury's published per-head figures for every region.

issues.title: Per-head spending is not need-adjusted and covers only about three quarters of spending
issues.detail: The Treasury's regional tables allocate 'identifiable' spending to places: £957bn of £1,288bn (74%) in 2024-25. Defence, debt interest, overseas spending and other items are not allocated. Attribution follows Treasury rules, not necessarily where the money is physically spent.
issues.impact: A higher figure for a region does not mean it is better treated; age, health, deprivation and rural costs differ. Quoting a league table of per-head figures would mislead.
issues.handling: The page says so beside the figures and shows population, age structure and deprivation next to spending.

issues.title: Deprivation indices exist for England only, and are relative
issues.detail: The English Indices of Deprivation 2025 rank areas within England. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland publish their own indices built differently. Ranks say how an area compares with other English areas, not how deprived it is in absolute terms. Region scores here are the population-weighted mean of district scores.
issues.impact: Deprivation cannot be compared across the four nations, and a mean can hide very deprived neighbourhoods inside an affluent district.
issues.handling: Deprivation is shown for English regions and districts only and labelled as English.

issues.title: Region names and table shapes differ between sources
issues.detail: The Treasury calls the region 'East' where ONS says 'East of England'. In the Treasury's regional tables the data starts on the row directly under the year headings, with no outturn/plans row, so a parser written for the other tables skipped the first region (North East) without any warning. Nomis allows only 25,000 values per request without a key.
issues.impact: One region silently missing from every regional chart; population requests failing part way.
issues.handling: Name mapping is explicit; the loader now skips a row only when it is a genuine outturn/plans row; population is requested in age chunks.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: DWP's accounts workbook agrees with the Treasury, but contains lines that look out of place
issues.detail: The 'Total departmental spending' line in the DWP annual report workbook (£323,501m for 2025-26) matches PESA's DWP total (£323,388m) to within 0.04%. The workbook also shows apprenticeships (£3.1bn) and adult skills (£1.4bn) as DWP sections, which are not what most people expect of a work and pensions department.
issues.impact: Readers may think DWP runs skills programmes it no longer does, or doubt the figures.
issues.handling: Shown as published with a note that responsibilities move between departments; a check requires the two sources to agree.

issues.source: DWP spend over £25,000 (csv) and DWP statistics
issues.title: The underpayment figure is only part of the story
issues.detail: Underpayments in the published table (£1.2bn for FYE 2026) are official-error underpayments. Since FYE 2023 underpayments caused by claimants (previously 'claimant error underpayments') are reported separately as 'unfulfilled eligibility', which is not loaded yet.
issues.impact: Presenting £1.2bn as the amount people were underpaid would understate it.
issues.handling: The UI labels the figure as official-error underpayments only. Loading unfulfilled eligibility is backlog item B-03b.

issues.source: DWP fraud and error statistics (Tables 3, 4, 8 and 9)
issues.title: Error reasons overlap, and the underpayment tables are labelled 'Official Error'
issues.detail: A case can have several reasons, so the reasons in Table 3 add up to more than the benefit's total (Universal Credit: £8.1bn of reasons against £6.7bn overpaid). The columns of the underpayment reason tables (8 and 9) are headed 'Official Error' although the table titles say they are underpayments.
issues.impact: Adding up reasons would overstate the total; the headings could be read as overpayments.
issues.handling: Each table's own 'Total' row is used as the total and checked against the time series (every benefit matches); reasons are never summed, and the underpayment columns are treated as underpayments, following the table titles.

issues.title: Unfulfilled eligibility is a separate estimate, not a correction to the overpayment figure
issues.detail: Unfulfilled eligibility (£3.7bn, FYE 2026) is what claimants could have been paid had they told DWP accurately about their circumstances. It is measured on a different sample basis and published separately, and DWP withholds many cells ('w') where cases are too few.
issues.impact: Netting it against the £9.9bn overpaid would give a number DWP does not publish; the benefit rows add to slightly more than the all-benefits figure (rounding and benefits not measured every year).
issues.handling: Shown beside overpayment and official-error underpayment as three separate measures with ranges kept in the database; never netted.

issues.title: Losses, special payments and liabilities exist only as PDF text and do not fully itemise
issues.detail: The notes on losses, special payments, contingent liabilities and the audit opinion are not in the accompanying workbook. The itemised lines add up to £0.6m less than the losses total and £1.3m less than the special payments total (2024-25 gaps are larger: £5.4m and £1.7m).
issues.impact: Treating the listed lines as the whole would understate losses; mis-keying a figure would go unnoticed.
issues.handling: Lines were transcribed by hand with page numbers into registry CSVs; the loader refuses unless the lines do not exceed the published total and leave under 2% (or £2m) unexplained, and stores the gap as an explicit 'Not itemised' row.

issues.title: The auditor qualifies DWP's accounts on regularity every year, because of benefit fraud and error
issues.detail: The Comptroller and Auditor General gives a clean opinion on the accounts being true and fair but a qualified opinion on regularity: overpayments of £9.7bn and official-error underpayments of £0.8bn (excluding State Pension) are irregular because they do not conform to the legislation. The auditor's figures differ slightly from the national statistics (£9.9bn all benefits including State Pension).
issues.impact: A qualified regularity opinion is about legal conformity of benefit payments, not about the department losing money to suppliers; readers could confuse the two.
issues.handling: Shown as the auditor's own wording with the page reference, beside the statistics, with a note that the bases differ.

issues.title: The register contains no dissolved companies, and mass-registration addresses are huge
issues.detail: Status counts in the file: 5.17m active, 423,006 'Active - Proposal to Strike off', 108,330 in liquidation; dissolved companies are not in it. One Covent Garden address (71-75 Shelton Street) is the registered office of 81,569 active companies and about 27% of all active companies sit at an address shared with 50 or more others.
issues.impact: 'Shared address' alone says almost nothing about a company, and a status indicator cannot say how many companies have already gone.
issues.handling: Base rates are computed over this file and labelled as such; the shared-address indicator is shown with its 27% base rate.

issues.title: Risk-context indicators are defined and base-rated but not validated
issues.detail: Seven indicators are computed (docs/RISK_INDICATORS.md). None has been tested against published enforcement cases. One (renamed at least twice) is 8 times as common among paid suppliers as among all companies, mostly because large organisations are renamed in mergers, which shows how easily an indicator can mislead on its own.
issues.impact: Unvalidated indicators shown against named companies could harm lawful businesses.
issues.handling: Public pages show definitions and base rates only. Per-company indicators exist behind ANALYST_MODE=1, default off. Validation is backlog item B-17.

issues.source: Health and Social Care spend over £25,000 (csv)
issues.title: Almost all the money goes to other public bodies, mainly NHS England
issues.detail: In 2025-26 the files total £181.9bn (75% of DHSC's £244.1bn). £165bn of it is one recipient, NHS England, and the file's own 'supplier type' says 99% of the value goes to government bodies ('Govn'). Private suppliers and small firms account for about £1.2bn.
issues.impact: A reader would see a list of recipients dominated by one body and learn nothing about what the NHS actually spends on; the real spending happens inside NHS England, trusts and councils, which publish separately.
issues.handling: Shown as first-hop payments with the recipient type; the page says so. NHS England and trust spending is backlog item B-19a.

issues.source: Health and Social Care spend over £25,000 (csv)
issues.title: The file includes capital injections, loans and money coming back
issues.detail: Besides spending, lines record public dividend capital and loans to NHS bodies (£6.2bn) and, as negative amounts, dividends, interest and loan repayments received (-£1.3bn). 1,386 lines are negative in 2025-26 (reversals as well as receipts).
issues.impact: Adding every line overstates 'spending' by the capital and loan lines and understates it by the receipts.
issues.handling: Separate categories: 'Capital injections and loans to NHS bodies' and 'Dividends, interest and loan repayments received (money coming back)', shown apart from running costs.

issues.source: Health and Social Care spend over £25,000 (csv)
issues.title: Column names change case, some months are restated, and the supplier is sometimes blank
issues.detail: Headers alternate between 'Date' and 'Payment date', 'Expense Type' and 'Expense type', 'Supplier Post Code' and 'Supplier post code'; the first column is called 'Family'. Several months' files carry 'amended', 'revised' or 'corrected' in their names, meaning earlier versions were replaced. About £0.9bn (244 lines) in 2025-26 has no supplier or says 'Not Available'.
issues.impact: Fixed-name loaders break; a reader cannot tell which version of a month they have; unnamed recipients cannot be linked to companies.
issues.handling: Columns are matched on prefix ignoring case; only the published (latest) file per month is used and its name is recorded; blank and 'Not Available' suppliers are grouped as '(SUPPLIER NOT STATED)' and shown as such.

issues.title: Student loans paid to the Student Loans Company are not like other spending
issues.detail: £22.2bn of the £120.2bn in 2025-26 goes to one recipient, the Student Loans Company, to fund student loans. Loans are mostly financial transactions that are expected to be repaid in part, and are treated differently in the Treasury's accounts.
issues.impact: Mixing loan advances with grants and running costs overstates what the department 'spends' and hides the much smaller cost attached to loans being repaid late or never.
issues.handling: A separate category 'Student finance (Student Loans Company)', with a note that it is mostly loans.

issues.title: Large files, inconsistent labels and a typo-ridden vocabulary
issues.detail: 377,173 lines for 15 months (about 25,000 a month, 66 MB). The entity appears as 'Core' and 'CORE'; expense types include 'Other Goods and Services' and 'Other Goods & Services', 'Grant Expenditure' and 'Grant Expediture'; the June 2026 file has nine extra empty columns; one attachment is named 'Transapency'. 'Various' appears as an entity and as a supplier (£721m).
issues.impact: Counts of types and entities are inflated by spelling; a '£721m recipient called Various' cannot be identified.
issues.handling: Header matching ignores empty columns; categories are decided by regular expressions over recipient and expense type; 'Various' and similar are shown as '(SUPPLIER NOT STATED)'.

issues.title: Recipient type is guessed from names
issues.detail: The files say 'Grants Expenditure' for £95bn without saying to whom. We group by words in the recipient's name (council, academy, trust, university, college...). Names that match none stay as 'Other grants (recipient type unclear)' (£5.4bn).
issues.impact: Some recipients will fall in the wrong group (for example a construction firm paid a capital grant, or a trust that is not a school trust).
issues.handling: The category rules are in build_spend.py; the unclassified share is a live metric; recipients are linked to Companies House so a reader can check what they are.

issues.title: Spreadsheets, not CSV, with mixed date styles and some mistakes
issues.detail: Each month is an OpenDocument spreadsheet (.ods) with the month as the sheet name. Dates appear as true dates, as day-first text (21/01/2025), as dotted text (24.01.2025), as month-first text, and with typos ('04.07.205', '09/012026', and a payment dated November 2026 in a March 2026 file). 14 lines could not be dated reliably.
issues.impact: A standard CSV reader cannot open them; dates guessed the wrong way round move payments between months.
issues.handling: A small dependency-free reader parses the spreadsheets. Where a text date could be read two ways the reading inside the file's month wins (this rule is applied to the MoD only: for cumulative files such as the IOPC's, earlier months are legitimate and the day-first reading must stand, which a test showed; impossible or future dates are set to the first day of the file's month and counted).

issues.title: Only a fifth of the Ministry's spending is visible, and a third of lines are under the threshold
issues.detail: Payments in the files total £15.2bn for 2025-26 against £75.5bn of Total Managed Expenditure (20%). 41% of lines are under £25,000. Equipment under construction, nuclear and estates dominate; military pay and pensions are not supplier payments. A separate series covers purchase-card spending over £500, which is not loaded.
issues.impact: The files cannot show where the defence budget goes; much of it is pay, pensions and classified activity.
issues.handling: Coverage is shown beside the figures with a warning; purchase-card data is a backlog item.

issues.title: Some lines are accounting balances, not payments
issues.detail: The expense type 'CL MonthEnd Accruals Balance' (£468m in 2025-26, 1,467 lines) records month-end accounting entries. Foreign military sales appear as payments to 'UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT' (£496m).
issues.impact: Counting the accruals as paid out overstates payments; counting government-to-government items as suppliers hides the purpose.
issues.handling: Accruals have their own category, 'Accounting accruals (not payments)'; the US Government is left as a named recipient and flagged as a public body in the supplier linking.

issues.title: Entity names are misspelt
issues.detail: 'Ministy of Defence', 'United Kingdon Hydrographic Office', 'United Kingom Hydrographic Office' and the abbreviation 'UKHO' all appear for two bodies.
issues.impact: A count of bodies is inflated and totals by body are split.
issues.handling: Left as published; recipients are what we aggregate on, so totals are unaffected.

issues.source: Claimant context: Census disability, UC Health, take-up
issues.title: Census disability covers England and Wales only, and excludes about a million people
issues.detail: The Nomis table totals 58.56m people for England and Wales against 59.6m usual residents in the 2021 Census; the difference of about 1.0m is consistent with people living in communal establishments (care homes, student halls, prisons) not being in the table's universe, though we have not confirmed this. Scotland (National Records of Scotland) and Northern Ireland (NISRA) publish their own censuses and are not loaded.
issues.impact: Disability shares are understated in areas with many care homes or students, and Scotland and Northern Ireland show no disability figure.
issues.handling: The page labels the figure 'Census 2021, England and Wales' and leaves Scotland and Northern Ireland blank. Backlog B-34.

issues.source: Claimant context: Census disability, UC Health, take-up
issues.title: 'Disabled under the Equality Act', 'UC health condition' and 'on a disability benefit' are three different groups
issues.detail: Census disability is self-reported in March 2021 (long-term condition limiting day-to-day activities). Universal Credit 'health' claimants are people assessed or awaiting assessment for limited capability for work in June 2026 (3.56m, 42.6% of all UC claimants). PIP is awarded after assessment of the effect of a condition on daily living and mobility and is not income-tested. People can be in any combination of the three.
issues.impact: Dividing one by another gives a rate that sounds precise but is not a take-up or prevalence rate.
issues.handling: The page shows the measures side by side with each definition and date, and does not compute 'claimants per disabled resident'.

issues.source: Claimant context: Census disability, UC Health, take-up
issues.title: Spending per disabled resident would be misleading, so it is not shown
issues.detail: Social protection spending is mostly State Pension and benefits not aimed at disabled people, so dividing a region's social protection by its disabled residents gave about £41,500 for London, a number with no meaning.
issues.impact: A confident-looking ratio that invites wrong conclusions.
issues.handling: Removed on purpose; per-person spending by purpose is shown next to disability and health-claim rates instead. A true per-claimant figure needs claims by benefit and area (Stat-Xplore, B-32).

issues.source: Claimant context: Census disability, UC Health, take-up
issues.title: Open DWP tables are published from Stat-Xplore as OpenDocument spreadsheets, with ranges split across cells
issues.detail: The Universal Credit Health tables are open .ods files labelled as Stat-Xplore extracts, giving counts for 362 Great Britain areas with area codes (Northern Ireland is not covered). The take-up tables put confidence ranges as text across cells ('(1,550,' and '1,730)'), use [x] for not estimated (FYE 2021, the pandemic year) and [low] for suppressed counts.
issues.impact: A spreadsheet reader that expects numbers reads text, and the 2021 gap looks like missing data.
issues.handling: The dependency-free ODS reader and a range parser handle these; not-estimated years are left empty.

issues.source: Claimant context: Census disability, UC Health, take-up
issues.title: Take-up is estimated for only two benefits, and Housing Benefit take-up covers pensioners only
issues.detail: DWP's income-related benefits take-up release for FYE 2024 estimates Pension Credit (62%, range 59% to 64%, about 820,000 entitled people not claiming) and pensioner Housing Benefit (85%). Take-up is not estimated for Universal Credit, PIP or most other benefits in this release, and the take-up characteristics tables (PC2 onward) are not loaded.
issues.impact: The platform cannot yet say what share of people entitled to most benefits claim them.
issues.handling: Shown for the two benefits beside the overpayment estimates; other tables are backlog item B-35.

issues.title: The 'paid another way' share in the flow diagram is a remainder, not a published figure
issues.detail: The Treasury publishes how much of each purpose is bought from suppliers (gross current procurement, Table 5.5, and gross capital procurement, Table 5.6; they total £344.3bn and £117.0bn and agree with Table 5.3). It does not publish what the rest is made of. We call the remainder of each purpose 'paid out another way' (staff pay, benefits and pensions, grants, subsidies, interest and some accounting items). Procurement is gross of income, while purpose totals are not netted in the same way, so the remainder is approximate.
issues.impact: The 62% 'paid another way' is a minimum description, not a measurement of any one thing, and should not be quoted as 'benefits'.
issues.handling: The diagram labels the group 'Paid out another way (pay, benefits, grants, interest)', the story says it is a remainder, a table view shows the numbers, and checks confirm the procurement totals tie to Table 5.3.

issues.source: Energy Security and Net Zero spend over £25,000 (csv)
issues.title: Published nine months late, so 2025-26 is only partly covered
issues.detail: The department's £25,000 files stop at December 2025 (published September 2026). For 2025-26 they therefore cover April to December: £8.8bn of the department's £42.1bn (21%). The separate '£500' series on the same collection page is only purchase-card spending, a few thousand pounds a month. Six of the nine monthly files have no entity column filled in, and expense types are spelt in several cases ('Grant-in-aid To Arms Length Bodies', 'Grant-In-Aid to Arms Length Bodies').
issues.impact: A part-year can be mistaken for the whole year, and the figure for the energy budget looks far smaller than it is.
issues.handling: The page shows the months covered and the share of budget; case differences are ignored in categories; blank entities are left blank.

issues.source: Energy Security and Net Zero spend over £25,000 (csv)
issues.title: Many lines are accounting entries or investments, not spending
issues.detail: Largest lines are grant-in-aid to arm's-length bodies (the Nuclear Decommissioning Authority £3.1bn, Ofgem), equity injections into NNB Holding (Sizewell C, about £1.7bn), accounting entries for receivables, accrued expenses and cash transferred to the Treasury, and promissory notes for overseas aid (including a £515m payment recorded against the Bank of England).
issues.impact: Adding every line would present investments and bookkeeping as spending on energy policy.
issues.handling: Separate categories: 'Accounting entries (receivables, accruals, transfers): not spending' and 'Equity and loans (investments)'; grant-in-aid is a first-hop payment to bodies that spend it onward.

issues.title: One file covers two budget groups and has only four columns
issues.detail: MHCLG publishes date, supplier, description and amount only: no entity, expense type, cost centre or transaction number. One file covers both MHCLG groups in the Treasury's tables (local government, and housing and communities). Council names are abbreviated ('BIRMINGHAM CITY CNCL', 'GTR MANCHESTER COMBINED AUTHORITY') and the department name appears as 'MHCLG' and in full.
issues.impact: There is no way to split the payments between the two groups, or to see which part of the department paid.
issues.handling: The file is loaded once and the second group's page shows the same payments with a note; coverage compares it with both budgets together; the description doubles as the expense type.

issues.title: About £13bn of the 'payments' are business rates coming in from councils
issues.detail: Lines named 'BRR Central Share Income', 'BRR Central List Income' and 'Collection Fund Surplus' are the central government share of business rates, paid to the Exchequer through the Office of the Paymaster General (£14.0bn of the £45.0bn listed in 2025-26). They are income to government, not spending. 1,098 lines are negative (reversals and a zero-balance clearing account).
issues.impact: Counting them would roughly double MHCLG's apparent grant spending and make the Paymaster General look like its largest supplier.
issues.handling: A separate category 'Business rates: central share (money coming in from councils)' keeps them apart from grants; the page notes that the recipient is a pass-through.

issues.title: Only 7% of HMRC's budget is supplier spending
issues.detail: Payments over £25,000 total £2.5bn in 2025-26 against £33.3bn of Total Managed Expenditure. Most of the rest pays people (benefits such as Child Benefit and childcare schemes administered by HMRC), staff, and accounting items. Supplier spending is dominated by IT: Capgemini £404m, Fujitsu £267m, Accenture £183m, Cognizant £116m, and 'project mandays' lines. 487 lines are credits; 16% of lines are under £25,000.
issues.impact: The files describe how HMRC buys technology, not what the tax and benefit system pays out.
issues.handling: Coverage is shown beside the figures; IT project lines have their own category; benefit payments are a future item with the HMRC statistics (B-19e).

issues.title: Treasury files are tiny against a budget made of debt interest and financial transactions, and use another date style
issues.detail: 1,189 lines worth £217m for 2025-26 against £32.4bn of Total Managed Expenditure, because that total is mostly debt interest, financial sector items and accounting entries rather than supplier payments. The largest payment is £88m of Help to Buy ISA bonus prepayments to National Savings and Investments. Dates are written 04-Apr-25 and files start with a byte-order mark; the entity is HMT, DMO, GIAA or UKGI.
issues.impact: Reading the Treasury's supplier payments as its spending would understate it hugely.
issues.handling: The date style and byte-order mark are handled; coverage is shown; ISA bonuses and coinage have their own categories.

issues.source: NHS England spend over £25k and accounts
issues.title: NHS England's payment files show about a sixth of what it spends
issues.detail: In 2024-25 the files list £30.5bn of payments over £25,000, against £189.1bn of 'purchase of goods and services' in NHS England's accounts. £151.0bn of that (80%) is 'funding to group bodies': cash drawn down by integrated care boards (ICBs), a transfer to the local bodies that commission care, which does not pass through the payments ledger the files come from. The files are also published about ten months late (the newest, September 2025, appeared in July 2026).
issues.impact: The files alone would suggest NHS England mainly buys specialised hospital services and training, and would hide that most of its money goes to ICBs.
issues.handling: The NHS England page opens with the accounts breakdown, shows the share visible in the files, and labels the ICB funding as a transfer. We have not confirmed with NHS England why the transfers are outside the files.

issues.source: NHS England spend over £25k and accounts
issues.title: Where the NHS money finally goes comes from accounting categories for 2024-25, not from payments
issues.detail: To go beyond NHS England, we use the operating-expenses note of its 2024-25 accounts, which consolidates NHS England with the ICBs: £189.2bn including £86.7bn from foundation trusts, £40.3bn from other NHS trusts, £20.4bn from non-NHS providers, £13.7bn GP services, £10.5bn prescribing, £3.7bn dental and £2.2bn pharmacy. The note was transcribed by hand from the PDF (page 149); its 24 lines add up exactly to the published totals, and the loader refuses to run if they ever stop doing so.
issues.impact: These are totals by type of service, not payments to named organisations, and are a year old (2025-26 accounts are unpublished). Individual ICB and trust accounts are not loaded.
issues.handling: Shown as a separate chart, labelled 'accounting categories, 2024-25', with the year and source beside it. Individual ICB accounts are a backlog item.

issues.source: NHS England spend over £25k and accounts
issues.title: Spreadsheets with changing headers and many credit lines
issues.detail: Files are .xlsx. The expense type column is 'Expense Type' in some months and 'Expense Type for Report' in others, the amount is 'AP Amount (£)', sheet names change ('Sheet 1', 'A3131 report final'), a column of invoice numbers comes and goes, one file is marked 'corrected', and dates arrive as spreadsheet dates. About 6% of 2024-25 lines are negative (credit notes and reversals); in 2025-26 every line under £25,000 is negative.
issues.impact: A fixed-layout reader breaks or drops columns; summing positive lines only would overstate payments.
issues.handling: Columns are matched by prefix, the first sheet is read, negatives are kept so totals are net of credits, and the published corrected file is the one used.

issues.title: The Foreign Office's files stop at January 2025
issues.detail: No file has been published for February 2025 onwards, so there is nothing for 2025-26. The ten months we have (April 2024 to January 2025) list £7.5bn against £12.5bn of 2024-25 budget (60%). Files list invoice lines (45,057 lines in 9,942 payments), have no expense area, and one month names its date column 'Posted Date' instead of 'GL.Date'.
issues.impact: A reader would take the department as covered when it has no recent data, and counting lines as payments overstates the number of payments about fivefold.
issues.handling: The page says the latest data is for 2024-25 and compares it with the 2024-25 budget; the coverage page flags the department as stale; lines are counted as lines within payments.

issues.title: Aid goes to international organisations, so the end use is not visible
issues.detail: The category 'Aid' (£5.0bn over the ten months) is the main aid marker; 'Other Non-ODA Programme' marks spending that does not count as official development assistance. The largest recipients are GAVI, the World Bank (IBRD), the World Food Programme, UNICEF, the United Nations and the World Health Organization.
issues.impact: The files show who received the money first, not what it was finally spent on, and they cannot split bilateral from multilateral aid beyond the category.
issues.handling: Shown as 'International aid and contributions (mostly UN agencies and development banks)'; a first-hop warning appears beside the recipients.

issues.title: A title row, text dates and a stray note
issues.detail: The May 2026 file starts with a title line ('Annex A - Over 25000 transaction for May 2026') before the real header. Later files write dates as '01 June 2026'. The amount column is headed ' Amount ' with spaces. One line has the sentence 'This is cost relates to legal work' in the entity column.
issues.impact: The file is rejected or read with the wrong header; 683 lines would lose their dates.
issues.handling: The loader looks for the real header up to six rows down, reads day-month-name dates, and keeps stray text as published.

issues.title: Large lines are accounting entries, loans and funding for publicly owned companies
issues.detail: Of £2.0bn listed for 2025-26, £0.7bn is accounting entries ('utilisation of provisions', receivables) and £0.1bn is loans. The largest recipient is Post Office Limited (£752m) and the next UKRI-Innovate UK (£300m) and British Steel (£85m).
issues.impact: Treating the total as spending on business support would overstate it, and funding to a publicly owned company is not the same as buying a service.
issues.handling: Separate categories for accounting entries and for loans and equity; grants shown apart; recipients linked to Companies House where possible.

issues.title: Cabinet roles and remit groups are hand-curated
issues.detail: dept_map.csv lists role titles, not current office holders, and the remit groups are our own grouping.
issues.impact: Machinery-of-government changes will make the mapping stale; users may take our grouping as official.
issues.handling: The mapping is data, not code, and the pipeline fails if a PESA department is unmapped. Review is still manual.

issues.title: Only twelve bodies' transactions are loaded
issues.detail: Rules for categories and group bodies were written against DfT, the Home Office, DWP, DHSC, DfE, MoD, DESNZ, MHCLG, HMRC, the Treasury, FCDO, DBT and NHS England. Other departments will have other schemas, expense-type vocabularies and publication patterns.
issues.impact: The loader has been tested on thirteen publishers (CSV, ODS and XLSX) and each needed its own changes, so the next will too.
issues.handling: Each new department is loaded separately and will extend the rule lists.

issues.title: Several sources have only been checked for reachability
issues.detail: Contracts Finder, Find a Tender, ONS beta API, Parliament Bills API and the OBR page returned HTTP 200 without a key. Their formats, paging and licences have not been reviewed.
issues.impact: They may need work or limits we have not seen.
issues.handling: Listed as probed_ok in registry/sources.yaml, which is not the same as ingested.

issues.title: A report listed here is not a finding of waste
issues.detail: The list holds every NAO report: value-for-money studies, but also routine reports on a department's accounts, overviews and guides. Value-for-money reports vary from praising to highly critical.
issues.impact: Counting reports, or treating a listing as evidence of waste, would be misleading and unfair to departments that are audited more often because they spend more.
issues.handling: Reports are shown with the NAO's own type label, date, link and one-sentence summary, with no score or ranking. The finding itself is only in the linked report.

issues.title: Only about a third of reports attach to one of our departments
issues.detail: The NAO tags each report with the department it audited at the time. Cross-government reports, bodies outside our department list (arm's-length bodies, local government, the BBC, devolved administrations) and older departments that no longer exist are not attached.
issues.impact: A department page shows fewer reports than the NAO published about its area. Departments that merged or were renamed (for example Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy) are attached to their successor only where we mapped them.
issues.handling: The count of unattached reports is stated in the data notes; BEIS reports are mapped to Energy Security and Net Zero, which is an approximation.

issues.title: Summaries are the NAO's website text, not an extract of the findings
issues.detail: The one-sentence excerpt is written for the website and can be a plain description (for example of what an accounts report contains) rather than a conclusion.
issues.impact: A reader could assume the sentence is the conclusion.
issues.handling: The panel says so and links to the full report.

issues.source: NISTA Major Projects Annual Report data (csv)
issues.title: The file has no whole-life baseline, so project cost overruns cannot be calculated
issues.detail: Each project gives a whole-life cost, and a baseline and forecast for the current financial year only. 'Variance' is this year's forecast against this year's budget.
issues.impact: Presenting the in-year variance as an overrun on the project, or comparing earlier editions' baselines without checking definitions, would mislead.
issues.handling: The panel labels the variance as 'this year: forecast vs baseline' and says no lifetime overrun can be derived. Changes between annual editions are not computed yet.

issues.source: NISTA Major Projects Annual Report data (csv)
issues.title: Costs and ratings are withheld for a third of projects
issues.detail: 57 of 189 projects give no whole-life cost: 39 cite commercial-interest exemptions (alone or with others), others on national security, policy formulation, future publication, or because the project is still at planning stage. Ratings are exempt for some of the same projects.
issues.impact: Totals of whole-life cost and counts of red projects understate the portfolio, and Defence in particular is partly hidden.
issues.handling: Each department panel shows how many projects withhold costs and the stated reason in the row.

issues.source: NISTA Major Projects Annual Report data (csv)
issues.title: Delivery confidence ratings are judgements by two different assessors
issues.detail: Each rated project carries one rating, from one of two assessors: NISTA (formerly IPA) for 81 projects (24 red, 51 amber, 6 green) and the department's senior responsible owner for a different 91 (10 red, 58 amber, 23 green); 17 are unrated (exempt or too early). The two groups are different projects, so their mix of colours is not a like-for-like comparison.
issues.impact: Mixing the two ratings, or reading red as 'money lost', would mislead.
issues.handling: Each project's rating is labelled with who assessed it, and counts by assessor are shown separately rather than added together.

issues.source: NISTA Major Projects Annual Report data (csv)
issues.title: Whole-life costs span many years and are in 2024/25 prices
issues.detail: Costs are whole-life (sometimes 20 years or more) in 2024/25 real prices, with end dates given as low, mid and high estimates.
issues.impact: Adding them to annual payments or contract values, or comparing with cash totals, overstates spending in any one year.
issues.handling: Shown separately with the warning that it is not annual spending; the mid estimate is shown for end dates. Three non-ministerial bodies' projects (HM Land Registry, National Crime Agency, Valuation Office Agency) are not attached to a department.

issues.source: Public Accounts Committee publications (Parliament committees API)
issues.title: Committee reports are attached to departments by title only
issues.detail: The committees API does not say which department a report concerns. 273 of 805 reports are attached: some because the title names the department, others because the title is contained in the title of an NAO value-for-money report on exactly one department. Cross-government and topic-only reports stay unattached, and a name in a title can refer to a body other than the department.
issues.impact: A department page shows fewer committee reports than exist for it, and a few may be attached to the wrong department.
issues.handling: Each row says why it was attached; the NAO match is used only where the NAO tagged exactly one department. Recommendations and government responses are not loaded.

issues.title: Justice publishes fifteen separate files a month and only to February 2026
issues.detail: Headquarters, prisons and probation (HMPPS), courts (HMCTS), the Legal Aid Agency and eleven arm's-length bodies each publish their own monthly file under two yearly collections. 163 files, April 2025 to February 2026, are loaded (37,006 lines, £7.0bn). Two small bodies publish nil returns in some months; March 2026 is not yet published.
issues.impact: Totals for 2025-26 cover eleven months and are not comparable with a full year; a body that files late is under-counted for that month.
issues.handling: All fifteen publishers are loaded together under Justice with the originating body kept as the 'entity'; the panel says which months are covered; nil returns are dropped.

issues.title: Two-digit years, month-first dates and a mangled pound sign
issues.detail: Dates are written 25/04/25, and 454 lines are written month-first (06/09/2025 in a June file). Amounts carry a pound sign that decodes to a replacement character in the usual encoding; a few files add total rows or 'Nil Return' text lines (dropped, as they carry no amount).
issues.impact: Read naively, month-first dates fall in the wrong month or the future, and the pound sign breaks number parsing.
issues.handling: The loader reads two-digit years, resolves ambiguous day/month using the month of the file (these files each hold one month; this is only done for Justice and Defence), and drops lines with no date.

issues.title: Some suppliers are codes or redacted, and a few rows are misaligned
issues.detail: Some HMCTS lines carry a code instead of a supplier name (for example counsel fees, with the transaction number given as REDACTED), and three lines have text in the wrong column so the originating body is unreadable (£0.2m).
issues.impact: Rankings of top suppliers miss redacted payees; the entity breakdown has three stray labels.
issues.handling: Lines are kept as published. Supplier rankings should be read as excluding redacted payees.

issues.title: The January 2026 file is almost empty
issues.detail: Eleven monthly files, April 2025 to February 2026, hold about 10,500 lines (£4.2bn). The January 2026 file has only 18 lines (£1.6m) against about a thousand in other months.
issues.impact: Defra's 2025-26 total is understated by roughly a month of payments; the file may be incomplete or truncated at source.
issues.handling: Loaded as published and flagged; March 2026 is not yet published. Coverage figures are against the full-year budget.

issues.title: Defra pays its own arm's-length bodies and they publish in the same file
issues.detail: Grant-in-aid from Defra to the Environment Agency (£1.4bn), Natural England (£0.2bn) and other bodies appears as a payment, and the same bodies' payments to their suppliers appear in the same file under their own entity (for example the Environment Agency's £0.7bn).
issues.impact: Adding both counts the same money twice.
issues.handling: Payments to named group bodies are flagged intra-group and excluded from totals by default (switchable); the body's own supplier payments are kept. Entity names vary (EA and Environment Agency; NE and Natural England) and are shown as published.

issues.title: The December 2025 file has no header row, and earlier files have no entity column
issues.detail: April to November 2025 files start with a header and omit the entity; December 2025 begins directly with data and adds an entity column. Amounts in December carry pound signs and decimals, earlier months are whole numbers.
issues.impact: A strict reader rejects December or shifts its columns.
issues.handling: The loader recognises a headerless 10-column file and applies the known column order; the missing entity is filled with the department's name.

issues.title: Most of the money is grant-in-aid to UKRI and a subscription to Horizon Europe; the files stop in December 2025
issues.detail: Nine months (April to December 2025) hold 1,729 lines and £12.1bn: £7.6bn grant-in-aid to UKRI research councils and arm's-length bodies, £2.0bn paid to the European Commission (international research subscriptions) and £0.3bn returned to the Treasury. The 'over £500' series published alongside is government procurement cards only. DSIT's 2025-26 budget is £15.5bn.
issues.impact: The files show where DSIT sends money first, not who ultimately spends it: UKRI councils then fund universities and companies and publish their own files, which are not loaded. Coverage is for nine months.
issues.handling: Categories separate funding of research bodies, international subscriptions and cash returned; the recipient is shown as the first hop. Following UKRI onwards is a backlog item (a follow-on page like NHS England).

issues.source: Restart Scheme statistics and contract package area annex
issues.title: Restart statistics are cumulative and rounded; payments are for one year
issues.detail: DWP's tables give referrals, starts and job outcomes cumulatively from July 2021 to April 2026, rounded to two significant figures, and the statistics are 'in development'. Payments in the files are cash paid in 2025-26 and one provider is paid under two company names in one area (Jobs 22 Ltd and AKG UK in area 1b). The annex lists areas as groups of local authorities, some of which no longer exist as districts.
issues.impact: Dividing payments by participants or outcomes would mix periods and bases; cost per outcome cannot be derived from these tables.
issues.handling: The panel shows payments and statistics side by side with the periods labelled and never as a ratio; performance is shown only as job outcomes against the contract's own minimum and target, which share one basis.

issues.source: DWP Universal Credit Health statistics, tables 4 and 5
issues.title: Assessment decisions are rounded, include a transition backlog, and conditions overlap
issues.detail: Counts are rounded (to 5 for monthly decisions, to 100 for conditions); monthly decisions since 2023 include people moved over from the old Employment and Support Allowance, reported in a separate set of columns; a person can have several conditions, so conditions add to more than the decisions; 18% of decisions have no condition recorded.
issues.impact: Adding conditions, treating a rise in decisions as more illness, or reading an outcome share as the share of disabled people would mislead.
issues.handling: The panel says so, uses only the columns for all UC health decisions (the separate ESA-transition columns are not shown), and shows condition shares of decisions rather than of people.

issues.title: Civil servants are only part of the public workforce
issues.detail: The statistics cover civil servants (about 558,000 people). The armed forces, police officers, NHS staff, teachers, local government and public corporations are not civil servants and are in separate datasets.
