A department's staff here may be a small part of the people its spending pays for (the NHS and schools employ far more than the Department of Health or the Department for Education).
issues.impact: Reading a department's civil service headcount as everyone it employs or funds would be badly wrong, especially for Health, Education, Defence and the Home Office.
issues.handling: Every staff panel states the scope and names who is excluded; the other workforce datasets are in the backlog.

issues.title: Pay is gross full-time-equivalent salary, not cost, and grades are mapped
issues.detail: Salaries are annual gross pay for a full-time equivalent, rounded to ten pounds, before pension and National Insurance. Except for the Senior Civil Service, departments set their own pay and grading and the Cabinet Office maps them to five common levels. The highest-earner figure is the mid-point of a £5,000 band.
issues.impact: Salary cannot be multiplied by headcount to give a pay bill, and the same grade can be paid differently in different departments.
issues.handling: Labelled as median full-time-equivalent salary; no pay bill is calculated; pay is compared only within a grade.

issues.title: Rounding, confidentiality marks and a mislabelled table title
issues.detail: Every count is rounded to the nearest five, so totals agree only within rounding (departments add to the service total within 10 of 557,825). Small cells are shown as [c] (confidential) or [n] (not applicable). The published title of Table 12 says full-time equivalent but its columns are headcount, and Table 12A is the full-time equivalent version.
issues.impact: Sums can be out by a few; a missing cell is not zero; trusting the table title would mislabel headcount as full-time equivalent.
issues.handling: The measure is read from each column's own heading, suppressed cells are stored as missing with their symbol, and reconciliation checks allow for rounding (six new checks, all passing).

issues.title: A department here is not always one spending group
issues.detail: Statistics are by 'parent department' (with agencies shown separately). Ministry of Defence figures are civilians only; non-ministerial departments (for example Ofsted, the Food Standards Agency, HM Land Registry) and the three territorial offices are grouped with Small and Independent Bodies; Scottish and Welsh Government staff are devolved civil servants.
issues.impact: Comparing a department's headcount with its budget misses staff paid through arm's-length bodies and public corporations.
issues.handling: The mapping file `pipeline/cs_dept_map.csv` is explicit; unmapped parents default to Small and Independent Bodies and are labelled as such.

issues.title: Salary bands by department are not in the published tables
issues.detail: Salary bands (for example £30,001 to £35,000) are published for the whole civil service only. By department, the tables give median pay by grade and the highest earner's band. A finer breakdown is in an interactive data browser that is not a downloadable file.
issues.impact: We cannot show how many staff in each department fall in each salary band.
issues.handling: Department pages show headcount and median salary by grade instead, and the service-wide salary bands are shown on the Workforce tab (formerly People). Senior pay by post is in separate transparency data (backlog).

issues.source: Departmental workforce management information (csv, xlsx, ods)
issues.title: Monthly workforce returns are management information with a wider scope than the civil service statistics
issues.detail: Each department publishes a monthly return in a common 41-column template. It is internal management information, not reconciled with official statistics, and it includes the department's arm's-length bodies and some staff who are not civil servants. Health and Social Care shows about 43,000 on payroll against 10,700 civil servants in the Cabinet Office statistics; Defra shows about 32,700 against 13,300.
issues.impact: Comparing the two sources, or reading either as 'everyone the department employs', gives different answers.
issues.handling: Both are shown with their own scope and dates stated; the monthly return is labelled as not an official statistic; no figure is derived by combining them.

issues.source: Departmental workforce management information (csv, xlsx, ods)
issues.title: Months differ, files are patchy, and six groups are missing
issues.detail: The latest month is August 2026 for most departments, but May 2026 for the Treasury, June for Transport and Defra, July for Health and MHCLG, and Defence's file holds only January 2026. Justice leaves the cost columns blank. Defra's grades add to only half its payroll total. Home Office, Cabinet Office and the Law Officers' departments have no return in this template that could be found; Education, Business and Trade and Justice publish in different places.
issues.impact: Departments cannot be compared month for month, and some figures are incomplete.
issues.handling: The month is shown on every return; blank or partial cells are left blank and the gap is stated; missing departments show only the Cabinet Office statistics.

issues.title: An underspend against the Supply Estimate is not a saving
issues.detail: The Estimate is the amount Parliament approves, often with a margin for uncertainty. Outturn can be lower because of non-cash items (depreciation, provisions), because spending slipped to a later year, or because a demand-led forecast was too high. Annually Managed Expenditure estimates are forecasts of demand (for example Energy Security and Net Zero: £81bn estimated against £28bn outturn).
issues.impact: Reading the gap as money saved or waste avoided would be wrong, and so would reading an overspend as waste.
issues.handling: The panel shows voted and spent side by side with a plain statement that the gap is not a saving; the Departmental Expenditure Limit and Annually Managed Expenditure are shown separately because only the first is a cap.

issues.title: Twelve of seventeen departments are transcribed
issues.detail: Health and Social Care, Education and Justice have no 2025-26 accounts we could find on GOV.UK; Defence and Defra present the summary table differently and are not yet transcribed. The HMRC table lists Estimate before Outturn, which was corrected, and every department is checked so that DEL plus AME equals the total budget.
issues.impact: Five large departments have no voted-against-spent panel.
issues.handling: The panel simply does not appear for those departments; they are listed in the backlog.

issues.title: MHCLG is two spending groups in one set of accounts, and variances include virements
issues.detail: MHCLG's accounts show Housing and Communities and Local Government as two Departmental Expenditure Limits; they are added together and attached to MHCLG - Local Government. The published variance differs from estimate minus outturn by up to £1.9m in places because of transfers between budget lines (virements).
issues.impact: Small differences between the published variance and a recomputed one.
issues.handling: The loader allows 0.1% of the estimate for virements; both MHCLG groups use the combined figure.

issues.title: Cabinet Office spending in the Treasury's tables is about four times its accounts figure
issues.detail: The accounts' total budget outturn is £3.2bn for 2025-26 (£10.8bn in 2024-25), but PESA Table 1.11 shows £13.3bn (£26.9bn in 2024-25). The other eleven departments agree with PESA within 15%. A likely cause is Annually Managed Expenditure that PESA attributes to the Cabinet Office but which sits in separate accounts (for example civil service pension schemes), which we have not confirmed.
issues.impact: Cabinet Office totals differ by source; a reader comparing the voted-against-spent panel with the department's headline figure would see two different numbers.
issues.handling: Both figures are shown with their own source; the Cabinet Office is excluded from the automatic PESA comparison and listed here until the difference is explained.

issues.title: A recorded loss is not proof of waste or wrongdoing
issues.detail: Losses include write-offs of uncollectable debts, exchange differences, and 'constructive losses', where money was spent on something that delivered no value because a decision changed (a cancelled road scheme, a terminated IT contract). Some are the result of sound decisions to stop a project. Special payments include compensation Parliament has not specifically approved (for example Windrush compensation) and legal costs.
issues.impact: Treating the total as 'money wasted' would mislabel prudent write-offs and compensation owed to people.
issues.handling: The panel defines the terms, shows what each item is in the department's own words, and makes no ranking or judgement; the figures are audited accounts data.

issues.title: Four departments transcribed so far, with different scopes and groupings
issues.detail: Work and Pensions (its own panel), Transport, the Home Office and HMRC are loaded. Others have not been transcribed. Departments report either the 'core department and agencies' or the wider 'departmental group' (Transport's group is £398m against £123m for the core because National Highways and HS2 are in the group). Many small cases are grouped as one case, and only cases above £300,000 are listed individually. HMRC's figures exclude tax revenue losses, which are in its Trust Statement.
issues.impact: Departments cannot be ranked on losses, and the totals are not comparable with each other.
issues.handling: Each total names its scope; the panel says only notable cases are listed; no cross-department ranking is shown.

issues.title: Grants are a different kind of spending from supplier payments, and must not be added to them
issues.detail: Grants (about £160bn in 2024-25: £124bn formula and £36bn general) are paid to councils, schools, charities, universities and companies under schemes. Some grant payments also appear in departmental payment files as 'grants' lines (for example payments to academy trusts), so adding the register to the payment files would count them twice.
issues.impact: A combined total of 'payments plus grants' would overstate spending, and reading the register as procurement would mislabel grants as purchases.
issues.handling: Grants are shown in their own panel, labelled as not payments for goods and services, and never added to payment, contract or budget totals; the coverage page shows the grants column separately.

issues.title: The register is redacted, covers one financial year, and awards are not payments
issues.detail: The official statistics are based on unredacted data; the register leaves out some awards, so the Home Office scheme total is £14.7bn against £16.4bn in the statistics (the register is 97.7% of the official £160bn overall; Education, Health, MHCLG and DWP agree exactly). The register is for 2024-25, a year before the 2025-26 budgets shown elsewhere. 'Amount awarded' is the amount awarded, with award dates from 2011 to 2025 (a multi-year award is dated once), not cash paid in the year.
issues.impact: Grants cannot be compared directly with 2025-26 spending, and per-year recipient totals may differ from what was paid.
issues.handling: The panel states the year and that some awards are left out; checks confirm the register against the official totals (four departments exactly, overall within 5%).

issues.title: Recipient type is worked out from names and identifiers
issues.detail: The register gives a recipient name and an identifier (company, charity or education provider number) but not a type. We classify by identifier, then by words in the name (council, police, academy, trust, university), so some recipients are misclassified, for example police and crime commissioners or education trusts.
issues.impact: Type totals are approximate.
issues.handling: The panel labels the classification as approximate; company and charity links use the published numbers, not the classification.

issues.source: Major projects joined to contracts, payments, grants and reports by name
issues.title: Money is linked to a project only where something names it
issues.detail: No dataset says which payment or contract belongs to which major project, so a project is linked to an item only when its name appears as whole words in a contract title or description, a payment description or cost centre, a grant title, or a report title, within the same department. 47 of 189 projects have at least one link. Projects with generic or short names (under 12 characters) are never matched.
issues.impact: The linked figures are a floor, not a project's cost: most contracts and payments for a project do not name it. Matching can also pick up an unrelated item that happens to use the same words, and contract values are whole-life values or framework ceilings.
issues.handling: Every link is listed with its title and supplier so a reader can judge it; totals are never added to the project's whole-life cost or to each other; the panel says they are a floor.

issues.source: Major projects joined to contracts, payments, grants and reports by name
issues.title: A project named in an NAO or Public Accounts Committee report title is not evidence of a problem
issues.detail: Audit reports are matched on title words. A report may praise, criticise or simply describe a project, and many are routine accounts reports.
issues.impact: A listing could be read as a finding.
issues.handling: Reports are listed by title and linked, with the same plain statement as on the audit panel that a listing is not a finding of waste.

issues.title: Concentration is measured on the visible payments only, and a department's visible part varies from 7% to 93%
issues.detail: Supplier concentration uses payments over £25,000 to suppliers, in each department's latest published year up to 2025-26 (the Foreign Office is 2024-25). Grants, payments to other public bodies, student finance, business rates and accounting entries are left out. Departments' files show very different shares of their budgets (HMRC 7%, Defence 20%, Transport 93%).
issues.impact: A low top-five share for a department whose files show little says nothing about the rest of its spending, and shares are not comparable as measures of market power across departments.
issues.handling: Each figure says what it covers and its year; the page states that shares are of the visible payments.

issues.source: Payment files, contract notices and grants joined by business
issues.title: A business is a Companies House number or a name, and corporate groups are not joined
issues.detail: Payments, contracts and grants are joined by company number where known, otherwise by a simplified name. The ownership of corporate groups is not loaded (persons with significant control is backlog item B-13), so Kier Construction, Kier Highways and Kier Living are separate businesses. A short hand-made list groups names that share a brand (61 brands such as Serco, Capita, Kier); it is a convenience on the name only, not verified ownership. Joint ventures are kept apart and not attributed to a partner so they are not counted twice.
issues.impact: A group's total take is understated where it trades through several companies not on the brand list, and a brand match can include an unrelated company with a similar name.
issues.handling: The page says brands are matched on the name only; joint ventures are shown as their own line; the ownership data would replace the list.

issues.source: Contract award notices (Contracts Finder and Find a Tender)
issues.title: Contract shares depend on free-text procurement methods, and values are whole-life ceilings
issues.detail: The procurement method is free text from the notice (more than a hundred wordings). Direct award is taken as wording such as 'without prior publication', 'direct award', 'single tender' or 'waiver'; framework or purchasing-system call-offs are kept apart because they are usually competed or allocated under the framework's rules; the rest are competition. Counts are used for shares because values are whole-life values or framework ceilings, split equally where several suppliers share an award. SME status is as flagged in the notice.
issues.impact: Direct-award and SME shares are approximate; value shares would be dominated by a few very large frameworks.
issues.handling: Shares are by number of awards, labelled approximate; contract value is shown only as an equal share and never added to payments or grants.

issues.title: Contractor numbers come from management returns for 14 departments
issues.detail: Contractors, agency and interim staff are the 'non-payroll' lines in each department's monthly workforce return (Home Office, Cabinet Office and Law Officers' returns were not found; Justice leaves costs blank). Returns are not official statistics, cover arm's-length bodies, and use different months. Consultancy contract counts are blank or zero in many returns, which does not mean there is no consultancy.
issues.impact: Contractor shares are indicative and cannot be ranked precisely.
issues.handling: Each figure carries its month; missing departments show a dash; the page says the returns are management information.

issues.title: A concentrated or contractor-heavy department is not necessarily doing something wrong
issues.detail: Some markets have few suppliers (submarines, nuclear sites, rail franchises); some delivery bodies funded through payment lines (for example Salix and Gavi) appear as large suppliers though they are not commercial contractors; framework call-offs can look like many contracts to one supplier.
issues.impact: Reading concentration or contractor share as a verdict would be unfair.
issues.handling: The pages state this plainly and show the facts without ranking departments as good or bad.

issues.source: Payment lines and contract notices classified by service
issues.title: 'What kind of service' is worked out from words, and departments label things differently
issues.detail: Departments use their own ledger labels (some separate consultancy, professional fees, legal, agency staff and contractors; others use one 'professional services' line). One common set of ordered rules reads the ledger account text first, then the description, then the category as a last resort; a department's category only overrides where its name is unambiguous (for example rail franchise costs). The result is a convenience for comparing departments, not an audited coding.
issues.impact: Some lines will be in the wrong class, and the size of 'consultancy' depends on how a department words its ledger.
issues.handling: The share that could not be classed is shown on each department; labels are shown beside the classes so a reader can see what the department called it; classes are never presented as the department's own coding.

issues.title: 'Consultancy' and 'contingent labour' are not always consultants or temporary staff
issues.detail: The Foreign Office books aid-delivery payments (to UN agencies, charities and implementing partners) under project-management and consultancy labels, so its consultancy total of about £1.2bn is mostly programme delivery. HMRC records IT contractors supplied through large technology firms as 'contingent labour' (£884m, with Capgemini the largest). DWP's ledger files a facilities contractor under 'professional services - non-advisory'. Transport's 'non staffing' partner contracts are classed as consultancy rather than labour.
issues.impact: Reading the totals as 'spending on consultants' or 'on agency staff' would overstate or mislabel them.
issues.handling: Each page says so for the departments affected; the label is shown as the department files it; no judgement of value for money is made.

issues.title: Contract classes use the notice's CPV description and title, which are broader than ledger labels
issues.detail: Contract awards are classed from their CPV description, title and procurement category, so their classes are not identical to the classes for payments. Values are whole-life, split equally where an award has several suppliers.
issues.impact: A business's contract classes and payment classes can differ for the same work.
issues.handling: Payments and contracts are shown separately on a company card with their own headings.

issues.title: The latest year is provisional, the long series changes definition over time, and forecasts are forecasts
issues.detail: Outturn for 2025-26 is the ONS's first estimate and is revised; the OBR's long run since 1900 joins several official series (GDP and debt definitions differ before and after 1948-49 and 1974-75), and years from 2026-27 are the OBR's March 2026 forecast, not data. 'Net debt' includes the Bank of England in the long series and excludes it in the databank's headline series, so the two differ by a few points of GDP.
issues.impact: A claim about a record or a trend depends on the series and the year; small differences in rank are within revision.
issues.handling: Each result names the series, marks forecast years separately on the chart, and gives the year it describes; the rule for 'supported' is printed beside each claim.

issues.title: Counts are people or cases depending on the table, are rounded or suppressed in places, and the latest quarters are revised
issues.detail: The Home Office publishes some tables in people (main applicants plus dependants) and others in cases (main applicants only). Small cells are suppressed ('z', ':'), 2018 and 2019 route-of-claim figures are rounded to the nearest 100, and figures for recent quarters are revised in later releases. Calendar-year and 'year ending June' columns appear side by side.
issues.impact: A ratio built from a people table and a cases table, or from a rounded year and an exact one, can be off by a few per cent.
issues.handling: Each claim uses one table at a time and says whether it counts people or cases. The loader reads the sheet headers and keeps suppression markers as nulls, never as zero. Totals are reconciled to the Home Office's own summary tables (check: asylum claims, hotels and supported population agree with the Home Office annual report).

issues.title: 'Route of entry' is the Home Office's own classification and about 8% of claimants have route 'Other'
issues.detail: Asylum claimants are assigned a route before claim (small boat, clandestine, entered without relevant documents, visa types, other). The route 'Other' covers claimants whose route is not recorded. Small boat arrivals are counted when they are detected, and the person may claim asylum in a later period.
issues.impact: Shares of claimants by route depend on how many are 'Other', and a small boat arrival in one quarter can claim asylum in another.
issues.handling: We show the 'Other' group, and give the share with and without it where the threshold is close to the dividing line. 'Illegal entry' is shown as the Home Office's label for the route, not as a legal finding: claiming asylum is lawful whatever the route.

issues.title: Fraud in asylum claims is not measured in any open source
issues.detail: The Home Office, the NAO and the Public Accounts Committee publish no count or rate of asylum claims found to be fraudulent. Refusals, withdrawals and 'clearly unfounded' certificates are not measures of fraud.
issues.impact: A claim about the share of fraudulent asylum claims cannot be proved or disproved from open data.
issues.handling: Recorded as a claim that cannot be tested (IMM-11), with the nearest published facts shown elsewhere (age disputes IMM-12, grant rates IMM-09/IMM-10). Backlog item B-48 lists what would be needed.

issues.title: Migration estimates are provisional and have been revised by more than 100,000
issues.detail: From 2025 the ONS estimates migration using administrative and travel data. The first estimate for the year ending December 2024 was 431,000; the completed estimate is 331,000 (ONS Table 5). The latest periods are marked provisional (P) and revised (R) in the source.
issues.impact: Net migration for the latest year may change materially in later releases; it is not comparable with the pre-2022 method without care.
issues.handling: The provisional flag is stored with each period, shown in the notes of the claim, and the revision history is loaded (ons_migration_revision).

issues.title: Some cost figures exist only in NAO reports, rest on supplier-reported or Home Office estimates, and are hand-transcribed
issues.detail: The hotel spending, contract cost estimate (£15.3bn over 10 years), supplier profit margins and large-site costs are NAO statements. The NAO says supplier data are not audited by it and that Home Office estimates contain significant uncertainty. They are typed into pipeline/published_figures.csv with the paragraph and the quoted sentence.
issues.impact: These are the best published figures but are point-in-time (2022-23 to 2024-25) and may be superseded.
issues.handling: Every figure carries its report, locator and quote in the table published_figure; the loader refuses a figure whose source has no citation. Panels say which year each figure describes.

issues.source: Home Office annual report and accounts
issues.title: No single audited line for 'the cost of asylum'
issues.detail: The Home Office reports a budget line 'Asylum Support, Resettlement and Accommodation' (£4.18bn outturn in 2025-26) that includes Afghan and other resettlement. The NAO's £4.0bn for 2024-25 is for supporting people seeking asylum. Departmental payment files over £25,000 do not capture the main accommodation contracts completely (one provider's payments stop in July 2025 in the file).
issues.impact: Costs in different sources are for different scopes and years and cannot be added or compared exactly. Per-person and per-day figures are our own derivations.
issues.handling: Derived figures are labelled as ours with the inputs listed. Payments data are not used to total asylum costs.

issues.title: The backlog counted here is first decisions only
issues.detail: Claims awaiting an initial decision are published by the Home Office. People waiting for an appeal at the First-tier Tribunal (Ministry of Justice) and the stock of people whose claims were refused but who remain in the UK are not in this data.
issues.impact: A fall in the initial-decision backlog can coexist with more people waiting at later stages.
issues.handling: The claim notes say so. Tribunal data are in backlog item B-49.

issues.title: Age assessment figures cover only people whose age was disputed
issues.detail: The table counts decisions on people whose claimed age was doubted and who went through an age assessment. It is a subset of all claimants and the data begin in July 2025.
issues.impact: The adult share among disputed cases says nothing about the share of all claimants who misstate their age.
issues.handling: The claim and its notes state the scope.

issues.source: Home Office support data matched to local authorities
issues.title: Local authority codes change and some asylum seekers cannot be matched to an area
issues.detail: Supported asylum seekers are published by local authority and code. Areas that changed code after 2023 reorganisations, and some people recorded without an area, do not match the ONS population table.
issues.impact: A small share of people is left out of per-1,000 comparisons and the deprivation test covers England only.
issues.handling: The number of unmatched people is printed with the result.

issues.title: Visa tables count visas issued from abroad, not people arriving, and policy rules changed during the period
issues.detail: Entry clearance tables count visas issued (decisions) to main applicants and dependants. Extensions and in-country switches, arrivals, and people who never travelled are separate or not in the table. Dependant rules for care workers and students changed in 2024.
issues.impact: A fall in visas issued does not equal a fall in arrivals, and shares of dependants differ before and after the rule changes.
issues.handling: Claims state that a visa issued is not an arrival and show main applicants and dependants separately; in-country extensions are backlog item B-50.

issues.title: Percentile groups are of Income Tax payers, based on a survey, and the latest years are projections
issues.detail: Percentile groups rank only people liable to Income Tax (about 37 million), not all adults, by total income before tax (not salary). The Survey of Personal Incomes ends at 2023-24; years from 2024-25 are HMRC projections. Total income includes pensions, savings and dividends, and 2008-09 is missing from the series.
issues.impact: 'Top 1%' means the top 1% of taxpayers, who are not the top 1% of the adult population; comparisons with projections can differ from later outturn.
issues.handling: Claims name the survey year, say 'taxpayers', mark projected years on charts, and show the number of people in each group.

issues.source: ONS effects of taxes and benefits (ETB)
issues.title: ETB is a household survey with imputed taxes, and its totals do not match administrative totals
issues.detail: The ETB attributes taxes and benefits to households by assumption (for example employers' National Insurance and VAT by spending), values health and education at cost, ranks by equivalised disposable income, and under-records some benefits and high incomes. Scaling average per household by households gives about 9% more Income Tax than HMRC's 2023-24 receipts, about 40% less VAT (households only, not VAT on public sector and business purchases) and 32% less State Pension than DWP spending.
issues.impact: Shares, ratios and the direction of the net position are reliable indicators; pound totals from the ETB should not be added to or compared exactly with Treasury or HMRC totals.
issues.handling: Aggregates are labelled survey estimates, the check against HMRC receipts is in pipeline/checks.py with a stated tolerance, and claims use ratios and direction.

issues.source: ONS effects of taxes and benefits (ETB)
issues.title: 'Receiving more than paying' counts the NHS and schools as benefits
issues.detail: Table 16 counts a household as a net recipient if cash benefits plus the value of services (education, health, adult social care, subsidies) exceed all taxes it pays. Two thirds of the benefits households receive are services valued at cost.
issues.impact: Over half of people are in net-recipient households, but that is mostly children in school, health care and the State Pension, not unemployment benefits.
issues.handling: The claim and its notes say so, and cash benefits are shown separately from services.

issues.title: Benefit expenditure by age group covers DWP benefits only
issues.detail: The age split is of DWP benefit expenditure (mostly Great Britain); it excludes Northern Ireland, NHS, schools, social care, tax credits administered by HMRC before their closure, and Council Tax support paid by councils.
issues.impact: Not a complete picture of state support by age.
issues.handling: The claim names the scope.

issues.title: Who pays a tax in law is not who bears it, and Council Tax and business rates are not HMRC taxes
issues.detail: The grouping into individuals, consumers, employers and companies follows the legal liability. Economists generally think employer National Insurance falls largely on workers' wages, and VAT on customers and shareholders in varying shares. HMRC receipts exclude Council Tax, business rates and other local taxes.
issues.impact: Moving employer National Insurance between 'employers' and 'workers' changes the headline split; both groups are shown separately.
issues.handling: Each group is listed with its members and shown separately so a reader can regroup.

issues.title: The tax gap is an estimate with a margin of error
issues.detail: HMRC estimates tax owed but not paid from audits, surveys and models. It includes evasion, avoidance, error and the hidden economy and revises past years each edition.
issues.impact: The £ figure is not the amount recoverable and may be revised.
issues.handling: The claim says it is an estimate and gives the year.

issues.title: Only mid-2025 population by age is loaded, and 16 to 64 is not 'working'
issues.detail: The dependency ratio uses population aged 16 to 64 against 65 and over; state pension age is now above 65, and many people aged 16 to 64 are in education, caring, sick or disabled. No labour market data are loaded yet.
issues.impact: The ratio is a demographic indicator, not a count of workers and non-workers, and has no trend.
issues.handling: The claim carries no verdict; labour market and history are backlog item B-53.

issues.title: Tax paid and benefits received by nationality or country of birth are not published
issues.detail: No open dataset gives tax or benefits by nationality; estimates rely on linked data held by government and on modelling assumptions.
issues.impact: Any statement about immigrants' net fiscal contribution cannot be proved or disproved with this tool.
issues.handling: Recorded as a claim that cannot be tested (TAX-20), with the nearest data (visa categories, net migration, asylum support cost) in the immigration section. Backlog item B-54.

issues.title: Council finance returns are England only, submitted at different times, and two tiers share services
issues.detail: Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland publish their own finance statistics (not loaded). For 2025-26 about 377 authorities have submitted; the latest submitted year for each authority is used (2023-24 to 2025-26). In two-tier areas the county provides education, social care and highways and the district provides housing, waste and planning. Two authorities (Barnsley, Sheffield) changed ONS code in 2026.
issues.impact: Spending per head of two councils is comparable only if both provide the same services; a figure for a constituency in a two-tier area needs both tiers.
issues.handling: Per-head comparisons use all-purpose authorities only; district and county spend are both apportioned to constituencies; the code change is handled through la_code_alias; the year used is stored with every row.

issues.title: Council budgets are not published by constituency: they are apportioned
issues.detail: No official body allocates council spending to Westminster constituencies. We apportion each authority's net current expenditure to constituencies by the share of the authority's residents (Census 2021 output areas) who live in each, using the ONS best-fit lookup.
issues.impact: A constituency estimate shows what its residents' share of local councils' spending is, not what is spent in the constituency, and assumes spending per head is equal across the authority.
issues.handling: Tables and the explorer label constituency finance as 'estimated by apportioning'; authority-level figures are the published ones.

issues.title: Council Tax tables mix all-purpose authorities with districts and counties
issues.detail: Average Band D figures for all-purpose authorities include adult social care and parish precepts; shire districts report a district element and the county precept is added separately.
issues.impact: A bill cannot be read off one row in a two-tier area.
issues.handling: The claim compares all-purpose authorities only.

issues.title: Postcodes show where a recipient is registered, not where money is spent or who benefits
issues.detail: A payment is placed using the postcode in the departmental payment file, or if absent the supplier's Companies House registered office; grants use the recipient's postcode. Head offices of large recipients (NHS England in Leeds, defence contractors, consultancies) take payments that serve the whole country. About half of payment value has a usable postcode (47.6% of supplier-payment value; 83.5% of grants).
issues.impact: The distribution by constituency is a distribution of recipient addresses and is distorted by head offices. It cannot say where services are delivered.
issues.handling: Funding passed to other public bodies and accounting entries are separated as a kind and excluded from the headline claims; medians rather than totals are used for deprivation comparisons; the coverage table and the postcode basis are stored with each row.

issues.title: Postcodes are matched to the live May 2026 directory
issues.detail: Postcodes that have ended since 2021 or are mis-typed in payment files do not match. A postcode is placed in a single constituency, local authority and output area as the ONS directory records.
issues.impact: A small share of placed payments may sit in the wrong place after boundary changes; unmatched money is counted in the coverage table, not distributed.
issues.handling: Coverage is reported per source in place_payment_coverage.

issues.title: Census 2021 is a snapshot from March 2021, England and Wales only, and constituencies are best-fit
issues.detail: The census was taken during Covid restrictions (employment and unemployment differ from today) and before the 2022 to 2025 changes in migration. Constituency boundaries are the 2024 ones, assigned by the ONS best-fit lookup so an output area sits wholly in one constituency. Scotland (57) and Northern Ireland (18) censuses are published separately (backlog B-58). Industry and main-language tables are only published at larger areas and are not loaded.
issues.impact: Constituency figures can differ slightly from the Commons Library's, and do not reflect changes since 2021.
issues.handling: Every claim and table says 'Census 2021', counts are added from output areas so constituency and authority totals match exactly, and Scotland and Northern Ireland are flagged as missing.

issues.title: Constituency counts of benefit claimants: now from Stat-Xplore; Northern Ireland and some history are missing
issues.detail: DWP publishes small-area claimant counts through Stat-Xplore (API key required); the Commons Library republishes them but blocks automated downloads. Open alternatives are local authority totals of UC claimants with a health condition (loaded) and Census 2021 disability and care.
issues.impact: UC claimants for a constituency here are estimates apportioned from the local authority by working-age population; PIP, Attendance Allowance and Pension Credit by constituency are not shown.
issues.handling: The estimate is labelled and the PIP claim is recorded as cannot-test with the reason; the decision on a key is backlog B-32 and B-58.

issues.title: Stat-Xplore counts are rounded, residence-based, differ in period by benefit and need a key to refresh
issues.detail: DWP rounds counts (to the nearest 5 for small areas) and suppresses very small cells; geography is where the claimant lives (residence-based), on the 2024 constituency and 2021 local authority geographies; each benefit's latest period differs (UC May 2026, PIP July 2026, Pension Credit, Attendance Allowance, Carer's Allowance, State Pension, ESA, DLA March 2026, Housing Benefit March 2026, children in low income 2024/25, NINo years to March 2026). Barnsley and Sheffield appear under their previous ONS codes. The fetcher uses the key from ./.env, never prints it, sends about 150 table requests two seconds apart on first run and none on reruns (every response is cached by query).
issues.impact: Small-area figures can be off by a few cases; rates divide by Census 2021 population, so places that have grown since 2021 are overstated; benefits cannot be compared to the day.
issues.handling: Periods are stored and shown with every figure; rates name their denominator; the key is in ./.env only and the fetch is skipped when it is absent.

issues.source: Annualised benefit spend (our estimate from DWP Stat-Xplore)
issues.title: Benefit spend by area is our estimate (cases x average award x 52), not a published figure
issues.detail: DWP publishes counts and average awards by area, not pounds paid. We multiply cases at each benefit's latest date by the average weekly award and by 52 (Universal Credit: households x average monthly payment x 12). That is the yearly rate at that date, not cash paid in a financial year. Nationally the nine benefits come to about £309bn against £297bn in DWP's expenditure tables for 2025-26 (a forecast): State Pension, Attendance Allowance, DLA, Pension Credit, Housing Benefit and Carer's Allowance are within 5%, PIP 7% higher (caseload growth), Universal Credit 10% higher, and Employment and Support Allowance 27% lower (DWP's expenditure includes cases and payments outside the 2021-geography table). Different benefits are for different dates (March to July 2026). The mean award includes cases with nil payments where DWP counts them. Several benefits can go to the same person, so cases are not people.
issues.impact: Treat area totals as the right order of magnitude and good for comparing places; do not use them as audited expenditure or to say what an individual receives.
issues.handling: Every spend figure is labelled annualised and dated; the national table compares each benefit with DWP's own expenditure and checks.py fails if a benefit moves outside its stated tolerance; per-head figures use the 2021 population.

issues.source: DWP Stat-Xplore: what is not available
issues.title: Universal Credit claimants' ethnicity and earnings are not in Stat-Xplore; UC starts have no constituency or authority split
issues.detail: The People on Universal Credit database offers age, gender, employment indicator (whether the household has earnings), conditionality regime, duration and the move from legacy benefits, but no ethnicity field and no amount of earnings. The Households database gives the payment amount and the elements of entitlement, not earned income. UC starts are published only nationally and by Jobcentre Plus office and postcode district, so cannot be added up to constituencies or authorities (those two geographies are not offered). Benefit combinations (people claiming two or more benefits) are England and Wales only. The employment indicator (whether the claimant had PAYE or self-employment income in the month) is not filled for the latest month: in May 2026 every claimant is 'not available'.
issues.impact: We cannot say how many UC claimants are of any ethnic group or how much they earn from DWP's open data; ethnicity of benefit claimants appears only in survey sources (the Family Resources Survey), which carry sampling error. Benefit combination rates for Scotland are missing, not zero.
issues.handling: Not estimated or imputed. The Questions page states the gap; benefit combinations show as missing for Scotland and Northern Ireland.

issues.title: Sanction figures count claimants sanctioned in a month, not sanctions or people ever sanctioned, and the denominator matters
issues.detail: The UC sanction rates database lists every Universal Credit claimant in the month and flags whether a sanction was applied that month. A claimant sanctioned in several months is counted in each. About half of all claimants have no work requirements (health, caring, young children) or earn enough that no requirements apply, so they are rarely sanctioned: the share of all claimants (about 1.3% in May 2026) is much lower than the share of claimants who have work requirements (about 3.5%) or who are in the searching for work group (about 6%). Sanction decisions can be challenged and reversed; the published figure is the decision at the time. Rates for small areas are rounded and suppressed.
issues.impact: Quoting 1.3% as 'the sanction rate' understates how often sanctions are applied to those who can be sanctioned; quoting 6% as the rate for all claimants overstates it. Comparing areas is sound only for the same month and the same denominator.
issues.handling: Every sanction figure names the month and the denominator; the national panel shows the rate for each work requirement group from the crossed table.

issues.source: NHS England, DfE, Home Office, MoD and ONS workforce counts
issues.title: Workforce counts use different definitions and dates, and should not be added together
issues.detail: Headcount counts people; FTE counts full-time posts (a part-time worker is a fraction). NHS England staff (ESR, July 2026) exclude GPs, their practice staff, agency staff and social care; school staff are the November 2025 census of state-funded schools; police are 31 March 2026 for England and Wales; armed forces are 1 July 2026 for the whole UK; the ONS public sector employment table (to June 2026) is a survey-and-returns estimate in thousands, rounded. Some people hold two jobs and are counted twice within a source. The ONS 'NHS' line covers all UK NHS bodies and the ONS 'Education' line includes universities and colleges, so neither equals a single department-sourced file.
issues.impact: Adding NHS England + schools + police + armed forces + Civil Service would not give 'public sector employment'; the ONS total includes devolved NHS bodies, universities, colleges, local authority staff and public corporations.
issues.handling: Each source is shown on its own basis with its date. Comparisons to the ONS total are stated as proportions with the definitions in the notes; checks.py compares each file with the matching ONS line within a stated tolerance.

issues.title: Suppressed values and thousands separators in school workforce files
issues.detail: Cells are 'x' (suppressed), 'z' (not applicable), 'c' (confidential) or numbers with thousands commas ('1,768.36'). The constituency file begins with a byte-order mark. Pay is published only where enough teachers are in the cell.
issues.impact: Read naively, the numbers become text or zero.
issues.handling: Commas removed; markers become NULL, never zero.

issues.title: Police tables mix forces with summary rows, notes and dates written three ways
issues.detail: Each table lists forces, then England and Wales, England, Wales, regions, the British Transport Police, the National Crime Agency and central secondments. Row labels carry '[note n]' markers; dates are text ('31 March 2003'), spreadsheet dates or '31 March 2025 [note 10]'.
issues.impact: Summing every row double counts; the British Transport Police and National Crime Agency are national bodies outside the 43 territorial forces.
issues.handling: Summary and national rows are kept but identified by code; the pipeline strips note markers and parses all three date styles; the check compares the 43 forces with the published England and Wales total.

issues.title: Armed forces tables are wide worksheets with dates in the column headers and a 'break in time series' column
issues.detail: Each worksheet has the series down the side and quarter dates across, with occasional blank columns marking a break in the series. Dates are written '1 April 2012 (number)'.
issues.impact: Series before and after a break are not strictly comparable.
issues.handling: Dates parsed from the header text; break columns skipped; worksheet number and title are kept with every row.

issues.title: Derived tables are reproducible up to floating-point rounding
issues.detail: Rebuilding the derived tables (places, supplier links, claims) from identical inputs gives identical text, counts and keys, but sums of decimal numbers can differ in the 15th significant digit because the database adds in parallel and the order changes the rounding. Two near-equal values in a ranked list can therefore swap places between builds. Until October 2026 the supplier linking and some grouped summaries also picked an arbitrary row among ties (any_value), which changed the Companies House link of about 24 of 32,000 suppliers between builds; ties are now broken by name and number.
issues.impact: A figure shown to 3 or 4 significant figures does not change between builds. The Companies House link for a supplier with several equally good candidates is now stable.
issues.handling: Ties are broken explicitly (min and company number) and string lists are ordered; the incremental update was verified against a full build table by table.
